speechtext:

Mr. Gronchi will be arriving in Ottawa on Saturday, March 3, and will remain until Monday, March 5. Mr. Gronchi will be accompanied by his Minister of Foreign Affairs, Mr. Gaetano Martino.

speechtext:
I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. Will the minister intervene on behalf of the Indians of the
Caughnawaga reservation near Montreal and arrange to halt the entry into and destruction of homes and property of those Indians by contractors of the St. Lawrence Seaway Corporation at least until the question of compensation and alternative housing accommodation is settled?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY REQUEST FOR INTERVENTION ON BEHALF OF CAUGHNAWAGA INDIANS
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker; the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration will not intervene. This matter has proceeded according to law, as provided by this parliament at the last session, and everything that has been done about this matter has been done in accordance with the law. Every Indian whose property is affected has been seen individually by the legal adviser of my department, and the whole situation has been thoroughly explained. Proper and appropriate arrangements are being made between the seaway authority, my department, the band council and a committee appointed by the band itself to deal with this matter. I think it would be quite improper, sir, to give any impression that anything else was the case.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY REQUEST FOR INTERVENTION ON BEHALF OF CAUGHNAWAGA INDIANS
speechtext: Does the minister recall that on June 27 of last year-

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY REQUEST FOR INTERVENTION ON BEHALF OF CAUGHNAWAGA INDIANS
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY REQUEST FOR INTERVENTION ON BEHALF OF CAUGHNAWAGA INDIANS
speechtext: Does the minister recall that on June 27 of last year he gave an undertaking to this house, the spirit of which seems to be completely denied by his present attitude? In the light of that previous undertaking, will the minister not reconsider and at least arrange that houses be not destroyed until alternative housing accommodation is provided in the middle of winter?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY REQUEST FOR INTERVENTION ON BEHALF OF CAUGHNAWAGA INDIANS
speechtext: No houses are being destroyed until alternative housing accommodation is provided.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY REQUEST FOR INTERVENTION ON BEHALF OF CAUGHNAWAGA INDIANS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this question is supplementary to the question asked by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton). Will the minister inform the house what compensation has been given to the people who live on the Caughnawaga reserve whose homes and property have been confiscated for the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway through that reserve?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY REQUEST FOR INTERVENTION ON BEHALF OF CAUGHNAWAGA INDIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. gentleman was quite inadvertent in using the word "confiscated". There is no

Inquiries of the Ministry question of confiscation; it is an expropriation for which full and adequate compensation will be paid.
It was suggested that an interim payment should be made but I am informed that the Indians would prefer to have the final value determined before being paid. A valuation has been made on behalf of the seaway authority and a separate valuation has been made by my department. At the present time my department, in consultation with the council of the band, is engaged in discussions with the seaway authority with a view to seeing whether an agreement can be reached which will be satisfactory to each individual Indian who is in possession of land being expropriated. If such agreement cannot be reached, of course, the issue will, as is always the case with expropriations, be decided by the courts.

Inquiries of the Ministry The question continues: If so, will the minister state what the government decision is in the matter? speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration what progress has been made in providing facilities in Israel to deal with prospective immigrants to Canada, and also what relatives of Canadian residents will now be considered for such immigration?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: IMMIGRATION
subtopic: ISRAEL-FACILITIES PROVIDED AND APPLICANTS TO BE CONSIDERED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that perhaps this question should have been put on the order paper, but I do know there is a great deal of interest in the subject and I might just as well reply now. The government has made no progress in providing facilities for immigrants from Israel and has no intention of making any progress in that direction because the government of Israel, which is a country seeking immigrants, does not wish us to do so. We have provided consular service in Israel which is available to my department to assist in dealing with applications of certain categories of close relatives of Canadians who are admissible and desire to come to Canada.
Those categories are, in the case of residents of Canada, the wives or widows and minor children of residents, men over 65 years of age, women over 60 years of age, duly ordained ministers of religion and other persons whose normal and full-time vocation is devoted to the service of a recognized religion, husbands and parents, and humanitarian and compassionate cases. In the case of Canadian citizens resident in Canada, the list also includes children of any age, married or single, and fiances.

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, February 22, consideration of the motion of Mr. Howe (Port Arthur) for the second reading of Bill No. 82, to provide for short-term credit to grain producers in the prairie provinces to meet temporary financial difficulties arising from inability to deliver all their grain, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Nicholson.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday, during the discussion of this amendment, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) placed on the record an excerpt from a report published on February 3 of this year on "Agricultural Markets and Prices" by the provincial royal commission on agricultural and rural life in Saskatchewan. I drew the attention of members of the house to the fact that the minister had seen fit to place this one excerpt on record, yet had neglected to read further in the report and deal with the conclusions and recommendations made by that commission.
It was the minister himself who introduced this document into the debate, and it was simply for the purpose of setting the record straight that last evening I read into the record a portion of a conclusion arrived at by that commission with respect to the subject now under discussion. Hon. members will recall that last evening there was such

Grain
a babble across the way that I and other members in this group found it almost impossible to determine what hon. members on the other side were objecting to, although we could well judge from their behaviour that they found the remarks most unpalatable. Now I have had a chance of reading Hansard, and I note the requests of hon. members opposite to read all the sentences in the particular conclusions I placed on the record yesterday. In conclusion No. 17, found on page 207 of the report, the commission states as follows:
Delayed deliveries of wheat, necessitated by lack of storage space, result in high farm storage expenses and delayed returns to producers. For farmers with limited resources the resulting financial hardship is serious. The proposal that farmers be paid storage for farm-stored grain has considerable merit.
At this point I should like to draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that, when the Minister of Agriculture went to the press after the house adjourned, he himself did not place all the sentences on record. He just took one sentence out of that conclusion to buttress his particular point of view, but I draw to your attention this reference in the part I had not read yesterday:
The proposal that farmers be paid storage for farm-stored grain has considerable merit.
Then it goes on to say:
In addition, the provision of emergency credit by banks and credit unions-
Once again I want to draw to the attention of hon. members of the house that this legislation has completely ignored the credit union movement in the country.

guaranteed by the federal government, would be a useful part of any long-term agricultural program.
This is the part I put on the record yesterday, and note that the legislation before the house is presumably to take care of an emergency. It is temporary legislation. Yet the commission states:
In the meantime, advance payments could be made by the wheat board on properly stored grain on the farm to ease the farmer's immediate cash shortage.
If the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) had been interested in giving a comprehensive picture of the report to the house he could have gone on further from the conclusions to the recommendations, and on page 216 he would have found recommendation No. 14, which reads as follows:
That, in view of the grain producers' immediate need for cash and their present difficulty in selling farm stocks of grain, the federal government promptly establish, on an emergency basis, a system of cash advances on farm-stored grain.
May I draw attention to the words "on an emergency basis", because, if you will recall,
the earlier part I placed on the record uses the words "in the meantime". In other words, what the commission is actually doing is suggesting that there is a place in a longterm program for reenactment of the 1951 type of legislation, but nowhere in the report does it suggest that type of procedure as a solution to the present emergency situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Would my hon. friend mind reading recommendation 15, since he is in the mood for confession?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I think we could go on reading from the report for hours, but in my opinion the Star-Phoenix summed it up very neatly in its editorial of February 14 when it suggested that so far it looks like a draw between loans and cash advances. We will admit to the minister that there are excerpts he may take from the report which may give him some solace and comfort-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: He needs it.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
-but by the same token we can produce far more valid quotations from the report to prove our point. I suggest to the minister that this last-minute effort to clutch at the report as a means of alibiing for the impasse in which the government finds itself is not too convincing, and in that regard I should like to refer to what the minister said in his speech yesterday. As found at page 1447 of Hansard he said:
The bill was recommended by the farm leaders of the province. It is endorsed by a commission of the provincial government-
That was a deliberate effort to create the impression that because the commission, in an omnibus study of farm problems, happened to mention this particular issue, which was not such a serious problem at the time the commission was holding its hearings, somehow or other what they said represents the viewpoint of the provincial government. The minister went on to say:
-but it is opposed by this little group who represent perhaps some opinion but, if my opinion is correct, it is a small portion of the public opinion in the province of Saskatchewan.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that some time next June hon. members will have a chance to see, through the surest method possible, just how public opinion stands in that province. However, in view of the fact that the minister stated in the house yesterday that we do not represent public opinion in the west, I think the time has come to reiterate and place in proper perspective the recommendations of farm organizations throughout the west. I ask hon. members to weigh them in the balance and to decide just who is speaking for the farmers of western Canada. There are in the province three organizations which represent

Grain
the vast majority of the farmers there. I refer to the Saskatchewan wheat pool, a member of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the federated co-operatives, with membership throughout Saskatchewan and the province of Manitoba, and the Saskatchewan farmers' union. What do we find? I mention this in connection with the remarks of the minister yesterday. The Saskatchewan wheat pool held its annual convention last November and in their publication headed "Wheat Policy-1956" they have this to say: This stems from or is contained in the report of their 1955 convention held last September:
The current problem of a shortage of farm cash was considered as soon as the annual meeting opened. The delegates went on record in favour of a system of cash advances against farm-stored grain to be paid out by the Canadian wheat board through elevator companies with the federal government assuming the interest on the loans involved.
That is the announced policy of the Saskatchewan wheat pool. Yet the minister suggests that we are not speaking for organized agriculture in western Canada. Surely neither the minister nor any hon. member on the government side of the house can argue that the Saskatchewan wheat pool does not represent the vast number of farmers on the prairies. Then we have the 150,000 members of the federated co-operatives in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba. They have gone on record in this connection. In a resolution which was sent to the Prime Minister they state as follows:
Whereas we consider the recently announced plan to place cash into the hands of grain producers through government guaranteed bank loans is entirely inadequate and most unsatisfactory for the following reasons:
1.	The amount available through the proposed plan is not nearly sufficient to meet such immediate items as taxes, harvest operating costs and living expenses for the average grain farmer.
2.	It is unfair to ask farmers to pay interest on loans against their production when they are not responsible for the inadequacies of national policies that make it impossible for their grain to be sold on world markets.
Therefore, federated co-operatives, representing 650 consumer co-operatives with a membership of 150,000 in the province of Manitoba and Saskatchewan, request the federal government to arrange interest-free advances on farm-stored grain.
That is another argument. Does the Minister of Trade and Commerce suggest that the federated co-operatives are wrong? He has intimated that the wheat pool is wrong, that the federated co-operatives are wrong and that the Saskatchewan farmers' union is wrong.

He is the chief apologist for the government. In 1953 when this matter was before the provincial house-and I am glad to see that the hon. member for Rosthern has returned to his seat-this resolution was passed unanimously by the Saskatchewan legislature. I repeat that when the present resolution comes before the house I am satisfied that every Liberal M.L.A. in the house will vote for it just as they did in 1953. But out west the Liberals have one story. They have one voice out there. When they get down here it is an entirely different matter. I know that the hon. member for Rosthern in a recent broadcast which is printed in the Saskatchewan Valley News, a Rosthern paper, goes to bat for the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He does not try to beat about the bush. He comes out and parrots exactly the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. In this broadcast he quotes the minister as follows:
We looked at the possibility of advances to producers by elevator agents on behalf of the Canadian Wheat Board. At first glance this seemed to be a logical procedure, but the more we looked at it the less we liked it.
Then a little further on he quotes the famous passage from the speech of the Minister of Trade and Commerce:
You must be careful about lending on grain where only limited security can be had. The grain on the farm would be the only security the board would have. It may be said that the farmer would have to market the grain and bring it to the country elevator eventually, when the board
Grain
would be able to recover its loan; but I suggest that the farmer does not necessarily have to bring it to the country elevator.
In other words the hon. member for Rosthern is parroting the accusation made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that the reason they cannot bring in cash advances on farm-stored grain through the wheat board is that you cannot trust the farmer. When the hon. member for Rosthern will go on the air and say to his own constituents that the reason you people are not getting what the farmers want in the west, namely cash advances, is that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) does not trust the people of western Canada, he suggests that once the advance is made, they are going to cheat the wheat board and that they are going to try to peddle their grain elsewhere. Even if that were possible I think it is shocking that a statement like that should be made by the minister and even more shocking that those words should be parroted in the province of Saskatchewan by the hon. member who is in effect insulting his own constituents.

I have referred to the Saskatchewan wheat pool, the Saskatchewan farmers' union, the federated co-operative and the legislature of Saskatchewan. I could mention the Liberal politicians of the west. Mr. McDonald made the statement that this legislation was as effective as a stirrup pump in a forest fire. Mr. Prowse damned it with faint praise recently on a television program. Private members go out to their constituencies and label this legislation as being unpalatable. And yet, the Minister of Trade and Commerce tells this house that we are not accurate and are not voicing the feelings of our people back home. But beyond that, Mr. Speaker, I am quite willing to look into the grass roots to the thousands of people throughout the province who are sending in their representations.
A return was brought down in this house just recently, sessional paper No. 193, containing certain correspondence that was received in this connection. You will find that

those communications are from rural municipalities in the province of Saskatchewan, many of whom have reeves and councillors who are not supporters of the C.C.F. Many of them are quite active supporters of the Liberal party. I have been going through this return and I find communications from the Easton board of trade, from the rural municipality of Moosomin, from the constituency represented by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle federally, and also from the constituency represented by the leader of the Liberal party in Saskatchewan, from the rural municipality of McLeod, from the rural municipality of Buchanan, from the international woodworkers of America, the Prince Albert branch. We have representations from the Saskatchewan farmers' union, the wheat pool committees, and so on.
The following resolution was passed by the wheat pool committee held in Lanigan:
The Lanigan wheat pool committee unanimously agree that the proposed bank loans available to farmers, up to $1,000 at 5J per cent interest is definitely unsatisfactory and unjust.
This came in before the details of the new legislation were known. I continue with the letter:
The Lanigan wheat pool committee strongly recommend:
That the dominion government make an advanced payment of $1 per bushel on a 4-bushel quota on the 1955 crop.
The rural municipality of Manitou Lake wrote a letter along the same lines. There is a telegram from the farmers' union, subdistrict 5. There is also a letter from White-wood, Saskatchewan, containing a resolution of the east central motor dealers association. Quite naturally, the central motor dealers association are concerned about payments on their cars. They want to sell cars, and they know that so long as the farmer is not able to get cash for his wheat he is not going to be able to pay his bills.
There is a letter from Stoughton, Saskatchewan; there are resolutions from municipal councils and from the rural municipality of Happyland.
One could go through these letters by the hour and read over the resolutions that came from rural municipalities. There were so many representations, Mr. Speaker, that when this return was asked for permission was granted to summarize some of them. If that were not done we would have received a mountain of a return.
There were approximately 35 telegrams. This is a sample telegram from North Battle-ford, and reads as follows:
Resolved that the council of the rural municipality of North Battleford No. 437 go on record as

favouring cash advances on specified acreage of farm-stored grain in preference to guaranteed bank loans . . .
Thirty-five telegrams along that line were received. I find here a sample letter which more or less summarizes 165 letters received by the government along the same lines. I note here a letter from the rural municipality of Sutton, Saskatchewan. There were approximately 165 letters of this type received, Mr. Speaker. This letter is dated November 7 and reads, in part, as follows:
At the meeting of our council on November 1 the following resolution was passed unanimously:
"That we protest the proposed plan of guaranteed bank loans to farmers as being totally inadequate . . .
Then, there were petitions to the government of Canada. One hundred and nine of these were received containing 3,256 names in connection with the matter now before the house.
The other day the Minister of Trade and Commerce suggested that we are representing only a small group from the prairies. In the light of the representations that have been made from every responsible farm organization in my province-and they have asked in each instance for cash advances to the wheat board-and in spite of this mountain of evidence, the minister still persists in his attitude and belief that the government has some support for this measure on the prairies. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the silence of their own supporters is mute testimony of the unpopularity of this legislation. Do you mean to tell me, Mr. Speaker, that if we were wrong, that if we were sticking our necks out, we would not be jumped on by private members from the prairies? We have not heard from some of them. One or two have taken part in the debate. I say this with all respect to the hon. member for Ros-thern. He has been carrying the load for the government in this respect. He has been the work horse for the party in trying to put this unpopular measure across in the house. All credit should be given to the hon. member. But I find it very difficult to believe the Minister of Trade and Commerce thinks that we are in the wrong and they are in the right in view of the silence, whether it is enforced silence or voluntary silence on the part of his supporters, because if there was any great doubt in their minds about the feeling back home they would not lose any opportunity of jumping into this fight with both feet and belabouring the members of this group.
This debate has brought out only too clearly the fact that we have conscientiously, and I think faithfully, interpreted the wishes of agriculturists, the people who are represented by many members of this group. Although

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate is now in its tenth day and I can sympathize with the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hahn) when he wonders who is right and who is telling the complete truth. I can also sympathize with the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce), who spoke in this debate and placed the problems of his constituents before the house. Our two constituencies in the last two or three years have suffered comparable crop losses. Our problems are, I think, far more serious and far more difficult of solution than others which have been placed before the house.
The opposition has repeatedly stated before this house that there was unanimous agreement among the farm organizations and farm leaders as to how this money should be made

Grain
available to the farmers. I think that, in order to bring this debate into its proper perspective, the events leading up to the meeting with the federal cabinet in October should be reviewed, because the decision of the government concerning cash advances was made as a result of a delegation which came to Ottawa to present the problems of the western farmer to the federal cabinet.
When I think of this problem I recall a meeting that was held in Beausejour in December and was attended by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny) and the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dins-dale). At this particular meeting Mr. James Patterson, president of the Manitoba farmers' union, spoke at length on the matter of cash advances. I made rather comprehensive notes at that meeting and have since reviewed them. Mr. Patterson stated that the farm leaders were far from unanimous when they came to Ottawa to meet the federal cabinet. He stated they were far from unanimous when they discussed the matter at the Saskatoon conference.
Concerning the Saskatoon conference a special dispatch appears in the Winnipeg Free Press of September 28 which reported what transpired at the meeting. The following is reported:
Bank loans up to $1,000 based on grain to be delivered to elevators and guaranteed against loss by the federal government was suggested by President J. H. Wesson of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool as the means to alleviate the emergency financial problem of western farmers. He said the federal government should be asked to pass an act similar to that of 1951 which provided emergency financial assistance to farmers in difficulties. That year the crop was snowed under and farmers could not harvest.
Mr. Wesson said the Wheat Pool did not agree with the suggestion of interest-free loans to farmers, but the interest should not be exorbitant. The banks would grant some loans now, but were "choosey" of their debtors and the five per cent interest was too high. He thought the government should pass the legislation and there should be an arrangement between the Bank of Canada and the chartered banks whereby the loans to farmers be on a two or 2J per cent interest basis. The loans could be made on the basis of the grain the farmer would probably deliver and entered in his quota book. The federal government should take the loss, if any.
The following day a further dispatch appeared which reads as follows, and I quote from the Winnipeg Free Press of September 29:
The farm conference here Wednesday urged the federal government to make immediate provision for advances to farmers on grain they had in store, up to the value of half the normal delivery expected, or four bushels per cultivated acre. These should be repaid on the basis of one-half the value of each delivery made by the farmer.
The two-day conference was attended by governmental officials and representatives of farm, municipal and business groups from the three

prairie provinces. It was called by the Interprovincial Farm Union council to discuss grain marketing and possible financial assistance to farmers.
The resolution as originally presented contained a reference to not more than three per cent interest be charged on the advances to farmers. Jake Schulz, president of the Manitoba farmers' union, tried to amend the resolution by striking out the reference to interest and inserting a clause that the advances to farmers be interest-free.
Incidentally, I would state that was the farm union's original proposal and they have since stuck to it.
Others disagreed with the substituted clause and all reference to interest was deleted in the final draft. It was generally agreed the resolution should be broad so the federal government would understand the conference favoured the principle of advance and the method was under the government's jurisdiction.
Warren Burgess, who I understand is also an ex-C.C.F. member of the Saskatchewan legislature, had this to say:
.	.	. interest-free loans would give some big
farmers a chance to make money. Under the system as proposed by Mr. Schulz, a farmer not in difficulties, could apply for interest-free loans and then put the money advanced into government bonds.
For this reason J. E. Brownlee, president of the United Grain Growers, suggested there be a flat maximum for these loans or advances. Only those in need of the emergency assistance should get it. J. H. Wesson, president of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, had made the same suggestion Tuesday when he proposed re-enactment of the 1951 act which allowed loans up to $1,000.
Mr. Brownlee said time was the essence. The proposal should be presented at the federal-provincial conference next week.
A report appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune on the same date and the following observation was made:
It was generally agreed the resolution should be broad so the federal government would understand the conference was in favour of the principle of advances but wanted to leave the method up to the government.
At the meeting in Beausejour to which I previously referred, Mr. Patterson stated that when the delegation came to Ottawa they expected only to meet the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) but they were pleased when along with the two ministers they met the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the other senior ministers of the cabinet and received a very sympathetic hearing.
He stated the only thing the delegation could agree on was that cash was needed. When asked by the Prime Minister how much, they simply were unable to tell him. When it was asked how the money was to be made available to them they could not tell the Prime Minister, either.
The truth of this statement is borne out in the Canadian Federation of Agriculture News

Grain
and Information Bulletin of September-Octeber 1955 which in referring to the brief presented to the cabinet states:
The brief urged the government of Canada to "make immediate provision for advances to farmers on grain in store on the farm, and further that these advances should be up to one half the value of each delivery (of grain) made by the farmer".
The brief did not recommend any one way in which they thought these advances could best be made. Bank loans, wheat board advances, a special credit agency, and a system of advances through rural municipalities have been some of the alternative methods suggested.
It was recommended also that regular bank interest rates were higher than should be charged on such advances, and that the interest rate "if any", should be kept to a minimum.
This is also borne out in the press report of a speech made by the Minister of Agriculture for Manitoba in addressing the Union of Manitoba municipalities as reported in the Winnipeg Free Press of November 24, 1955:
Some idea of the confusion which existed at Ottawa when representatives of the three prairie governments and prairie farm groups met Prime Minister St. Laurent and some members of his government to discuss the western wheat crisis was given to the Union of Manitoba Municipalities by Hon. R. D. Robertson, minister of agriculture, Wednesday.
Mr. Robertson said when the prime minister asked him for suggestions, he had to admit they did not have one definite suggestion to make. As a result the representatives of 15 groups presented their personal views on the matter and most of them were different.
Mr. Robertson said he had attended a meeting in Saskatoon before the Ottawa meeting, but many of the resolutions could not be accepted by the representatives of the governments or other groups because they had received no instructions on them.

There seems to be some confusion on this point and perhaps I should do what I can to clear it up at the present time. The citation upon which such interruptions are based is citation 265 which reads:
It is not in order to read articles in newspapers, letters or communications emanating from persons outside the house and referring to, or commenting
on, or denying anything said by a member or expressing any opinion reflecting on proceedings within the house.
At the present time we are discussing the second reading of Bill No. 82 and any outside reflection upon proceedings in this house with respect to Bill No. 82 would be out of order under that citation. It is not out of order to read short extracts-I emphasize the word "short"-in support of an argument or a motion as long as they do not offend citation 265 or any other rule of the house. There comes a point however when if one were to read at great length-I am sure hon. members will agree-the assumption would be that the hon. member who has the floor was not making his own speech but, as I believe another citation in Beauchesne's third edition points out, was introducing another member into the chamber which of course our rules do not allow.
These rules are difficult to administer and the Speaker or Chairman gives a great deal of latitude to the hon. member who has the floor before interrupting him in order to be sure in his own mind that no injustice is being done to the hon. member. On the other hand, whoever is occupying the chair must consider that there are 265 members of this house and must try to preserve the rights and privileges of all members and keep everyone within the rules.
It was I who interrupted the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Wylie) yesterday, but I did so because in my opinion I thought the article which he was attempting to read was reflecting upon the proceedings of this house and, under citation 265, was contrary to a line of rulings which have been delivered by Speakers.
Of course, the interpretation of any rule is open to argument at any time, but fortunately or unfortunately, as the case may be, I am the person charged with making the decision. Since I did not interrupt the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Weselak) it was because I had decided in my own mind that he had not transgressed that particular rule. I trust that this somewhat extended explanation, for which I apologize, will go to some length to clear up this particular point in hon. members' minds.

The heads of the two national labour bodies- the Trades and Labour Congress and the Canadian Congress of Labour-Saturday agreed with farm unions that the need of such payments should be recognized.

of the disorganized approach to the problem by farm leaders the government had no justification for doing otherwise than to bring in the legislation it has proposed. After all, I only represent them here and I am only here because in a large democracy we cannot all gather together as they used to in the old days. I have been just imagining to myself a conversation with one of my constituents in Greenwood. I think that, when he found out the story, he would say to me that we in this parliament are being asked to act as no sensible men in consideration of their own businesses would ever be asked to act-in other words, without the evidence and without talking to the people concerned.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is now so long since I spoke on the* resolution that I can hardly convince myself-in spite of what I hear-that we are still discussing the question and if I may be permitted to say so, are straying about as far away from it as we can. At that time I took half an hour to try to convince the house that there is only one matter under consideration when we are dealing with Bill No. 82. It was not before the house then and I could understand the position taken at that time-the bill had not been seen-namely that there was a special condition which arose last fall and which required to be dealt with.
The government ^decided that the better way in which to deal with the question was to have loans made by the banks. The government decided that was the quickest, the cheapest and the most effective way of dealing with the question. There never was any decision made, when that point was reached, as to whether the final way to deal with the wheat question was to have advances made

on the grain that is on the farms. That question was not under consideration by the government at that time at all. The question under consideration was the quickest way of getting into the hands of the farmers cash which they could use in order to pay their accounts.
It was also well known that there were many who said that the quickest, the cheapest way and the best way from all points of view to have that done, was to have these loans put out by the banks. There were, of course, others who said otherwise. There were those who said that perhaps it could be done in some other way better than that. But the question that had to be decided by the government was this: Are we going to do it in some other way or are we going to have that particular thing done in the manner provided in this bill. It had no relation whatsoever at that time to the long-term policy of the government in relation to the handling of wheat or in relation to the handling of the surplus of wheat and so on.
As I stated, the decision was made to do it through loans obtained from the banks.
Back in 1951, there had been on the statute books an act which made certain provisions to do the same thing,-not for the same reasons but to do the same thing-namely to provide with cash the farmers who desired it and had to have it. Because there were very few of them who took advantage of it and because not a very considerable amount of money was involved-I think some $600,000 went out under that system-some suggestion was made that it did not do any good and had not any particular purpose. After all, some $600,000 is quite a lot of money. If put out in sums of less than $1,000, it takes care of a considerable number of farmers. From that point of view this legislation naturally suggested itself to a great many people. They said, "We have already had experience under it in 1951, and now it can be brought into effect again."
It is true that that legislation, as it was drafted at that time, was not functioning fully when the matter was discussed last fall. It was still in existence, and still on the statute books, but there was a termination date with respect to the time that it would operate. Hence it was suggested that we operate on a similar principle. That was at once taken to mean many things. Some people said, "It means that you can borrow only $1,000". Some people said, "The interest rate is going to be 5J per cent". As was indicated a few minutes ago by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Ellis), when he started to read his letters he found that some of those letters were written under those

Grain
circumstances when the question which was being discussed was not the question which is now before the house.
The present bill makes provision for loans up to $1,500. The present bill states that the interest rate is 5 per cent. The present bill also indicates a method by which the money is to be paid back, namely that half of the money obtained for the wheat from month to month over the period that the loans are out can be retained by the farmer with which to carry himself along. In other words, it is not the same legislation as that which was being discussed in those earlier days. This legislation is now known to the farmers and is understood by them. I therefore do not think we are gaining very much by going back and discussing what people thought at that time.
As a matter of fact, hon. members also know that-and probably I used the wrong term, as I am accused of doing sometimes- _ in the earlier part of the discussion when I made reference to regulations, somebody asked a question afterwards whether there had been any change in regulations and the answer was no. The fact is this, and everyone who knows anything about the situation out west knows it and if they presume to discuss the question from the western point of view they should know something about it, the fact is that the first statement which came out, and which was submitted by the banks to the farmers who applied for loans, was not satisfactory.
The Department of Finance called together a meeting in the city of Winnipeg. That meeting was attended by finance officials, by the solicitor for the wheat pool in Saskatchewan and by many others. They redrafted the statement which was put out to the farmers and reconsidered some of the conditions that had been put on under the first statement. One of them was as to whether the applicant agreed to pay taxes out of this loan before it would be made. Another one was as to whether loans that had been made by banks for other purposes should be taken under consideration. One was as to whether they had to examine the records at land title offices throughout the prairie provinces before they could make the loan. Those inconveniences were all removed within a few days and a new form was gotten out. Most of these resolutions that are paraded here in connection with this discussion were resolutions passed prior to the bringing out of these new forms, and the attitude today in the western part of Canada is not the same as it was at that particular time.
Then again it has been said that farm organizations believe this and that farm organizations believe that, and that you ought to call the farmers in here before a committee. There are 250,000 farmers growing wheat. To conceive of the idea of getting in a hearing before a committee of the house a sufficient representation or a more complete representation than is sitting in this house is just a proposal that could not be carried out in spite of the good intentions of my friend the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Mac-donnell). It might be good in theory but I venture to say that when you consider an organization that has 11,000 members-and that is true of one of the organizations that has been quoted-from among 250,000 farmers and when you figure that sometimes there are two or three out of the one farm house who belong to the farm organization, even an organization like that does not necessarily speak for the farmers of western Canada. Then, when you take another organization, as was done a few moments ago, which is not farming at all, as a matter of fact an organization which a very few months ago passed a resolution to the effect that they ought to be making oleomargarine, and quote it as an organization that speaks for farmers on every point, I would like to hear something that is a little more in line with what we would expect to decide our vote upon when we are considering a bill of this kind.
