maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
There is only one of them in Saskatchewan, so the hon. member will be able to find out all right.
The other matter which is of concern is this, Mr. Speaker. A few moments ago the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdon-nell) asked who were those people who were here to see the government. Well, it was the Canadian federation of agriculture, the largest farm organization in Canada and the most representative. After all, the farm organization that was mentioned a few moments ago has organizations in only four provinces of Canada. The federation of agriculture has organizations in every province in Canada. Not only have they organizations in every province in Canada but every single phase of agriculture from one end of Canada to the other is represented in that organization. When someone on the other side of the house said a few moments ago that that

Grain
organization is financed by the wheat pool, well, that answers a lot of the arguments that have been put forth in the house in the last few days. If that organization is financed by the wheat pool-and I am not saying it is -or by all the wheat pools of western Canada-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Who made the statement that it was?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: A speaker only within the last few minutes. The statement to the effect that it is financed by the wheat pools proves only one thing, namely, that if they were expressing the views of the wheat pools when they were down here, hon. members on the other side of the house have not been expressing them. I have not any doubt as to what the opinion of the wheat pool was as an organization.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: What about their convention?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I attend their conventions every year on invitation. I am a member of the wheat pool and I discuss all their questions with them for at least one afternoon every year. I know what their views are. I would call the attention of some hon. members to the fact that one of the members of this royal commission is a member as a representative of the wheat pool. Another is a member because he is president of the farmers' union, or was president when he was put on the commission. These men are members of the commission which brought out this report.
Some suggestion was made by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Ellis) that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) had tried to leave the impression that the government of Saskatchewan was in favour of these bank loans, because of what he said last evening. The Minister of Trade and Commerce did not say anything last evening which would give anyone justification for even making such a statement. He said that this report was being made to the government of Saskatchewan.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: He used the word "endorsed".

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
He said that this report was being made to the government of Saskatchewan by a royal commission which had been appointed by the government of Saskatchewan. I might say, in addition to that, if hon. members opposite think there were meetings held last fall they should have followed this commission around the province. This commission visited practically every hamlet in the province of Saskatchewan. It met farmers everywhere who would come and talk to them. After having done so IMr. Gardiner.]
they made the report which is on hon. members' desks, and it was submitted to the legislature in Saskatchewan since it met in its present session only about two weeks ago. That is about as up to date as anything one can get on the question.
Let us come back to where we were last evening. With respect to the result of the discussions which took place while they were out on the road interviewing everybody they could, doing just exactly what the hon. member for Greenwood says ought to be done, they say this, in arguing out the question:
The payment of advances on farm-stored grain would, in effect, be a prepayment of all or a portion of the initial price by the wheat board. Such a program would resemble, in a number of aspects, the commodity loan program of the United States.
They go on to say this:
One undesirable feature would be the questionable wisdom of making advances freely available to all' producers whether or not they are in need of financial assistance.
There could be nothing clearer than that. They say that is the objection to following the system, but then they go on to say:
The principal objection, however, lies in the field of administration. Provision would have to be made for inspection to determine adequacy of storage facilities, to verify quantity, and to determine grade. The additional costs involved would appear to make the proposal of doubtful value as a long-term program.
What hon. members are discussing more than half the time on this_ particular bill is the question of long-time policy. They are discussing that. This organization says that that particular thing might be most difficult to apply. I repeat, after having done that, after going out and hearing evidence all over the province, hearing all the farmers, that is the summing up of the matter. Then they say this:
Perhaps a more workable proposal is to reestablish the prairie producers interim financing act of 1951 on a permanent basis.
Well, if my hon. friends think that that is not good for the immediate time, are they prepared to accept it as a permanent policy of this government as something to be applied out west for all time ahead of us? Well, if they are, they ought to be very much more in favour of having it applied for the next six months to try it out. They pretend to be speaking here for the farmers of western Canada in saying that the farmers of that part of the country are opposed to this bill. Then they take this particular report of the commission and quote from it to try to prove that is the fact. I was somewhat astounded last evening when my hon. friend opposite the member for Regina City refused to read the opinion of this organization on the

question that was under discussion. He would read anything else but this. At the end of the quotation I have read, the commission goes on to say:
Therefore, the existing need could probably be met through re-enacting the prairie producers interim financing act as permanent legislation.
They refer to the existing need, not the permanent need. They say the existing need could be met by bringing that legislation into effect.
Let me turn to the conclusions at page 207 of the report. I am going to read all of conclusion 17.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I put it on record last night.
Mr Gardiner: No, you did not. You left out two sentences last night and ' you left out one today. I am going to read it all just as it is on page 207.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
May I
ask a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I will put it all on and you can follow it as closely as you wish.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: It is already on the record.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
No, it is not, not in the form in which I am going to put it on. I am going to put it on the record just as it is written in the report. Conclusion No. 17 reads:
Delayed deliveries of wheat, necessitated by lack of storage space, result in high farm storage expenses and delayed returns to producers. For farmers with limited resources the resulting financial hardship is serious. The proposal thai farmers be paid storage for farm-stored grain has considerable merit. In addition, the provision of emergency credit by banks and credit unions, guaranteed by the federal government, would be a useful part of any long-term agricultural program.
A survey-
Here is where my hon. friend came in last night and left out all that precedes this. He comes in with this:
A survey of present storage facilities is urgently required to determine whether new storage is needed and, if needed, where it should be built. In the meantime-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Yes, hear, hear. My hon. friend referred that "in the meantime" to the statement he did not read last night but that "in the meantime" does not refer to that at all.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Go ahead and read it.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
It says while they are making this survey of present storage facilities-
-advance payments could be made by the wheat board on properly stored grain on the farm to ease the farmer's immediate cash shortage.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
You are splitting hairs.
Grain

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I have not split any hairs, and if my hon. friend will sit down until I get through he can make any speech he likes providing he has not worn out his welcome already.
Now, the other statement which the hon. member for Regina was asked to read today and which he did not read-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: What sentence did I not read?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I am reading from page 216. Recommendation No. 15 (b) with regard to emergency credit is set in the commission's report:
(b) the recommendations with regard to emergency credit as set forth in the commission's report on agricultural credit be implemented or, alternatively, the federal government re-establish, on a permanent basis, the Prairie Producers1' Interim Financing Act of 1951.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Alternatively.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: That is the final recommendation that is made.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Read No. 14 now.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Yes, "or"; and my hon. friend goes on saying that the farmers are all against us. Well, I have had some very prominent farmers in my office within the last two days. Perhaps I should not say farmers, but very prominent individuals from Saskatchewan have visited me in my office within the last few days. These are men who are having farmers from the communities in which they live drop into their offices hour by hour and by the score, people who are doing daily business with them; and they tell me that the argument that is being put up here on the floor of the house is not correct at all.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Bank managers?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: None of them are bank managers at all. The main objection I heard was the objection I heard when I was in the west. I was in the west myself at the end of the week.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: You certainly were.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I was in Winnipeg, Regina, Lethbridge, Cardston, and in the Blood Indian reserve. I covered practically all of western Canada in my trip. The chief objection I heard to anything that is going on down here in the house was voiced by a gentleman in Winnipeg, who said the people in Melfort were hostile because the hon. member for Melfort refused to come home to discuss the on to the bay movement and was wasting his time down here making the kind of speeches he has been making. That is at least the opinion of a few farmers.

Grain

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Well, he was elected to come down here.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Eight thousand.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, 8,000 went before
Christmas and received loans amounting to some $7 million. Well, $7 million is not something to be laughed at. What is the effect of this bill in relation to that?
I might have agreed last fall with some of the things that were said, including the suggestion that perhaps we ought to call the house together, although there were not a sufficient number of people saying that to have placed a great deal of emphasis upon the contention that we ought to call the hon. members from all across the country to consider the terms of the new bill that was going to be brought in. However, I am quite convinced that the people back home and the hon. members who come here from all across Canada would have considered that 
a great waste of money not only by the government of Canada but by the individual members who had to come here to decide on one particular matter.
Therefore the government said to those concerned, "Well, in all probability when the house does meet it will pass this legislation", and in spite of what has been said and all the fighting that has been done I know it is going to be passed and there is no question about it.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Crack the whip.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
My hon. friends wonder how we can say that. We can say that as a result of the last election in Canada, and we will still be able to say it after the next election. So I want to say to my hon. friends that it was not considered to be the best policy or in the best interests of this country to call in over some 270 members of this house and the members of the Senate in addition in order to determine a matter which everyone knew at that time would be passed by this house.
We are here now asking hon. members to pass this bill and our hon. friends by talking for ten days on it-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: It has not been ten days.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: -and by saying they are going to go right on talking as long as they have breath left with which to talk about it and remain within the rules of the house, are serving no particular purpose. I do not like to sit here listening to them; nevertheless I do it.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Wasting time.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: We have to hear what they say in any case in order to be absolutely certain they do not say something different when they go home; therefore we sit here and listen to them. Hon. members opposite are here endeavouring to tell this house that the farmers out west are raising a terrible row about this. There is no one in this country I know of who opposes the government who hesitates to say to me all the nasty things he can whenever he has occasion to do so.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Give them a chance.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: But you keep moving around.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Give them a chance? I went right across the prairies last week end and I am going back again right across the prairies out as far as Calgary. I expect I will hear some more comments concerning the fact that my hon. friends are wasting their time and ours in Ottawa when they might have been getting this bill through

Grain
and into operation. The only thing they are accomplishing at present is to make bank managers hesitate here and there across western Canada before making loans. That is all they have accomplished in the last ten days. A farmer goes into a bank and says, "I want a loan," and the manager says, "Those members of yours in Ottawa are not going to put the bill through".

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I thought you said it was going to go through anyway.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I am sure it is, but hon. gentlemen on the other side of the house have been doing everything they possibly can to make sure that it does not go through. They are trying to convince the farmers back home that it is not going to go through. I would like to suggest to you that one of the reasons some of the farm organizations are losing membership so rapidly is because the farmers do not agree with what some hon. members are saying.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: We are not worried.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
The farm organizations in western Canada are not raising a row about this legislation. The only place I have ever heard any row raised about it was when some of my hon. friends of the C.C.F. group on the other side were getting meetings organized. They say that they did not organize them, that they just sprang up, but the fact is that they were getting them organized out there all across the country and were talking against loans. There have not been any other meetings of farmers in western Canada where resolutions have been passed.
The farmers of western Canada want to make use of this bill; not all of them of course, because all of them do not need the assistance provided by this bill. But the farmers in western Canada who are in greatest need of assistance want this bill and they want it as soon as it can be put through. I see the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort (Mr. Bryson) shaking his head. Well, I saw people in Melfort shaking their heads back in 1931 when they got $5 per acre when they had grown a lot of wheat. I know that farmers up in that section of the country are not supporting the position which is being taken by members in this house.
When the election is held in western Canada, as it will be sooner or later, I imagine that there will be fewer words said about this legislation than about anything else that has been under consideration in this country. Why will that be? That is if it is left to my hon. friends opposite to say the words. They are saying that members from Saskatchewan, from Manitoba and from Alberta ought to 67509-94
get up and talk about this legislation. They are simply telling you, Mr. Speaker, that they have not convinced the rest of the members of the house that they are giving us a proper report on western Canada. They are appealing for support of hon. members on this side of the house in order to put over a plan which they have in their minds. When they go back and try to explain the fact that for ten days they have asked the people of Canada not to provide loans to the farmers out west, that for ten days they have been threatening somebody that they should change their minds down here those members will change their minds.
A few minutes ago the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) spoke and said that they do not grow much wheat in his constituency. I think he could have said that they could not grow any wheat in his constituency. The wheat growers of the west are dependent upon men in his constituency. Most of the men interested in the financial institutions of western Canada live in Toronto and Montreal. Those men have looked over the whole situation and they are prepared to lend money to farmers under this bill.
Now we are told that we should not do it, that the farmers should not get it, that we should bring all the farmers down here before a committee to say what they think. If that were done there would be a lot of Tories who would be going back home and keeping quiet for the rest of the session. These farmers in the west have members here to express their point of view. If my hon. friends on the other side of the house are not able to express that themselves and are appealing to Liberals on this side of the house to express their views on the question, well may I say that I have expressed mine in a previous address on the resolution and I am expressing them again. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) was kind enough to say yesterday that I always have sufficient nerve-he called it courage but I will call it nerve-to speak to any meeting. I would not hesitate to go to any meeting in western Canada and meet any group of farmers and lay my point of view before them.
I repeat that the gentlemen who formed this royal commission were looked upon by the government of Saskatchewan as being the outstanding agriculturists in that province. They wrote this report and I have not any doubt that this report will be referred to in the debate that is going to take place as a result of the resolution introduced into the legislature which the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Ellis) read a few minutes ago. But

Grain
1 am just as sure that when the resolution is discussed this report will be discussed too. I have no doubt that there will be more support for this report in the legislature of Saskatchewan on both sides of the house than for what members are saying here.
This is a reasonable report got out by people who represented different organizations of farmers. One was a professor of agriculture at the university. Another member was a leader of one of the co-operative organizations that were referred to. Another was a member of the board of the wheat pool. Another was the president at one time of the farmers' union in Saskatchewan.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: And a farmer's wife.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, and a farmer's wife. That is a pretty good committee and they have made some very sound recommendations. One of the soundest recommendations was that there should be provision for farmers getting guaranteed farm loans from the banks in western Canada. That is what this bill proposes, and it proposes nothing else. My hon. friends go on discussing all kinds of things. The hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny) laughs at that, but I have said on one occasion before that this is not a laughing matter. This is a very serious matter with the farmers out west.
By this method they will be able to get money, and yet there are those who are trying to prevent them getting that. I repeat, no one on this side of the house, no one in the government, no one connected in any way with this measure has ever said that it will solve anything else but the matter of getting money quickly into the hands of farmers.
Then it will be found by the bill which comes up next that the government has gone on to say that it will pay storage on anything over the average amount of wheat which has been in the elevators for a term of years. Has anyone on the other side of the house made any objection to that? Of course they have not. They have all said they are going to vote for it. As a matter of fact I would rather expect that if some day some time there was some provision made for some kind of support for grain that has to be left on the farm, they will all support it. They will go even farther than that and say that when this bill was before the house they gave the government all the ideas that there are in existence in connection with this particular trouble.
I have watched them in operation. That is the way they always operate. They try to bring up everything they think the government may do some day so that they will

be able to say that they thought of it first. I am accustomed to that kind of argument, but the quickest way to satisfy the farmers of western Canada is to put this bill through and get it into operation so that when a farmer walks into a bank and asks for a loan the banker can say that with this legislation in effect he can give the farmer the assistance he requires.
The sooner that is done the better it will be for C.C.F. members. I should not say that because it might be worse for Liberal candidates if the C.C.F. members showed a little sense from now on, but nevertheless I give them that advice for what it is worth. Put the bill through, get it out of the realm of discussion among some 20 members of the house. Let us get on with our business.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in taking part in the debate on this amendment, following as I do one of the greatest orators, or I would like to say politicians Canada will ever know, I feel rather humble. But I am not prepared now, nor have I ever been and I hope I never will be, to accept his advice. I am ready to agree that if we must have a Liberal federal Minister of Agriculture perhaps the hon. gentleman holding that portfolio at the present time is one of the best we can ever expect to have.
I would like to point out to the right hon. Minister of Agriculture that you do not find many farmers interested in bank loans around the Bessborough hotel or the Fort Garry hotel or the Palliser hotel or the other larger hotels in western Canada. For that reason I was not too greatly impressed with the observations he made regarding the contentment that exists among the farmers of the west at the present time.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Not flying by T.C.A., either.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I would also like to point out to my hon. friends to my immediate right that we in the Social Credit group have not yet reached the position where we are prepared to take too much guidance from them. We did support this particular bank loan legislation in the resolution stage because in our opinion that was the proper thing to do. We did so because at that time we did not know the terms of the bill. When the terms of the bill were exposed to us, we ourselves changed our course and no one gave us any guidance. Let us keep that point clear. It was suggested that perhaps our position had changed. I would point out that on January

Grain
16, speaking in this house, I quoted from a report of the Social Credit caucus held in Edmonton, as follows:
The present federal policy with respect to loans on farm-stored grain is entirely inadequate and the proposal to put the farmers further into debt at 5 per cent interest is unfair and unjust when all the circumstances are taken into consideration. Not many farmers will be able to qualify for the full amount of the loan. Even if more of them did, the amount would not be sufficient in many cases to take care of the debts incurred in putting in and taking off the crop.
We believe the, federal government should make it possible for the Canadian wheat board to make cash advances to farmers against grain stored on the farm.
I maintain that that was our position at the opening of this discussion and has continued to be our position all the way through. We are in favour of this amendment which proposes to give it the six months' hoist, simply because we do not feel that the bill meets the wishes of the farmers of the west. Regardless of what the right hon. Minister of Agriculture has to say about farmer opinion in the west, we are not prepared to agree with him on that score.
We do not like the bill for several reasons. We feel the interest charge on these loans is far too high. Taking into consideration that the wheat board, for example can borrow at 3 per cent, we cannot see why farmers of the west should have to pay 5 per cent.
Again, the penalties for non-payment of the loan are in our opinion far too severe. Again, the bill itself does not give money to the younger farmers of the west who are just getting started. The other day I was able to convince even the Minister of Trade and Commerce that this was true.
During the course of the discussion, however, one very interesting thing has occurred. I am referring now particularly to the admission the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce made the other day in reply to the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch). The hon. member for Acadia was speaking about the storage problem under this bill, and he had this to say, as recorded on page 1315 of Hansard:
However, under this act he is not allowed to put that wheat into storage. Therefore, any farmer who has borrowed under this legislation, and who in order to get a fair grade tries to put his wheat into storage until such time as a grade has been arranged, puts the elevator agent in the position where he can be prosecuted if he allows the grain to be stored.
In reply to this comment by the hon. member for Acadia the Minister of Trade and Commerce had this to say:
I should like to say, if I may, that the department has taken cognizance of that fact and an
amendment will be offered if and when we get: the bill into committee which will make it possible to put grain in storage.
That did help some. On the other hand we still feel there are many features to this bill that are not worthy of our support. We are-still hoping, by the way, that the government will see fit to agree to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Acadia to refer this bill to a committee so that representations regarding it can be made by farmer organizations from the west.
This afternoon we have heard quite a debate as to what constitutes a farmer organization. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the wheat pools, the United Grain Growers, the-farmers' unions, and so on, have been mentioned. I maintain that if such a committee were established it would be only right and proper to ask all organized groups of farmers to come before that committee and submit evidence, and in that way this cross-fire we have to listen to here in the house would be eliminated.
In that connection, I have in my hand a copy of The Organized Farmer, which by the way is the official organ of the farmers' union of Alberta. We have been told that the farmers of the west are in favour of bank loans. With that statement I do not agree. I know the farmers of the west were opposed to bank loans from the day they were mentioned. Just to bring this point before you at the present time, I wish to quote briefly from the president's report in November issue of The Organized Farmer. I might point out that the farmers' union of Alberta is not a small organization of farmers; it is an organization that is composed of over 63,000 members, which is a good percentage of the farmers of Alberta. The president had this, to say:
The new plan for advances to farmers against, grain stored on farms has recently been announced. While this will be some help to farmers, the interest rate of 5 per cent is unreasonably high. There is a growing resentment among farmers against the idea of paying any such rate oi. interest for an advance on our own goods. Many farmers are strictly opposed to taking on a new debt and by so doing making more money for the banks. Why should not our government supply the money through our own Bank of Canada at cost? To go further, why should the wheat board not have access to the money at cost from the same source. It may be objected that this idea is "Social Credit" but so what.
The president went on further:
Of course the federal government will have to take the responsibility for the plan which they put out. If farmers refuse to use it the government will, of eourse, say that farmers don't need money. At the Saskatoon conference in September-

Grain
By the way, we have heard a tremendous amount about what happened at that particular conference. Here is the impression of this president:
At the Saskatoon conference in September, farm union representatives and the Saskatchewan minister of agriculture wanted to write a limit of 3 per cent into the plan to be presented to Ottawa. In fact most of them would have preferred to present a demand for a plan without interest at all. However, other opinions prevailed, and the brief presented asked for immediate advances without specifying any particular interest rate. I am now convinced that we should have stuck to our original idea and if the federation of agriculture and wheat pools, etc. would not have agreed, we should have presented our own plan to the government. In this case we conceded the point in order to present a united front for immediate action. In the long run, the other course might well have done our farmers more good.
Some fear has been expressed in parts of the house, Mr. Speaker, that in opposing second reading of the bill we are doing a great disservice to the unity of Canada. With that I cannot agree. All through the years this group has stood for all-out support to the primary industries of Canada. I am certain that throughout the years we have fought hard to improve the plight of eastern farmers. I am certain that we have supported the fishermen and others, and will continue to do so. It just so happens that the particular bill before the house is one that strikes primarily at the pocketbook of the wheat producer of the west. In that regard I ask the house to consider the fact that when the pocketbook of the wheat farmer of the west is affected it does not take very long for this influence to seep right down through the whole of the Canadian economy.
Why must we discuss bank loans? The reason is simply that the farmers of the west cannot market their wheat. We have been told time and time again that one of the reasons for the failure of the farmers to market their grain is the fact that there is a shortage of box cars in western Canada. I have in my hand a letter which I received in the mail this morning, and I wish to quote from it. It reads in part as follows:
The issue is rather confusing. Some places the [DOT]quota is 2 bushels per seeded acre, others claim 3 bushels. It doesn't matter very much what the quota is. Before a car can be shipped a permit has to be issued by the board, before the railways can supply cars. In talking with one of the C.N.R. operators-
This is a railway employee to whom he is referring.
-I was told that there wasn't any shortage of grain cars, permits to move grain was the hold-up. This fellow also said that not very long ago there were some 800 cars of grain sitting on sidings west of Edmonton waiting for orders to be .moved.
.
We are told, Mr. Speaker, that there is plenty of vacant space in the terminals on the west coast, so in my opinion this adds up to nothing short of inefficiency on the part of somebody, and perhaps even bungling. This afternoon the right hon. Minister of Agriculture was very impressive in pointing out to us that we did not know the opinion of the western farmers. Perhaps we do not know. Maybe he does not know, but I do know that last week a delegation came to Ottawa representing the interprovincial farm union council. In my opinion the interprovincial farm union council represents the best organized opinion of the farmers in five provinces of the dominion, and I only hope the day is rapidly approaching when this organization will represent the opinion of the farmers in the ten provinces. Here is what they had to say about this particular piece of legislation we are now discussing, first of all by way of review of what has happened:
Scores of mass protest meetings, resolutions and petitions that have developed spontaneously throughout the west accurately indicate the degree of dissatisfaction felt in rural areas regarding the guaranteed bank loans on farm-stored grain. It is felt almost unanimously that farmers should not be asked to burden themselves with added debt and interest charges because wheat is not being sold at a sufficient volume to enable the farmer to maintain his cash position.
They go further and discuss the bank loan program in detail. The bank loan program is not being used for a variety of reasons, and they mention such things as banking facilities. They say:
(a)	Banking facilities are not readily available in many parts of the prairie provinces.
I know that is definitely true in the province of Alberta. I also know that when the facilities of the Alberta government treasury branches were offered to the federal government, that offer was refused. They go on to say:
(b)	The amount of red tape involved in securing acceptance of a bank loan application is so great as to discourage all but the most persistent, and eliminates a good percentage of those who might otherwise qualify.
I should like to add one thing. Those who are most hungry have to go through this red tape as well.
(c)	Many prairie farmers today conduct their banking business with credit unions, and the government apparently has made no provision for loans through this source, but has limited its guarantee to the chartered banks.
(d)	The practice of banks deducting the value of any grain sold under the initial unit quota or additional small acreage quotas from the maximum face value of a loan means that most farmers can only qualify for amounts so small that they are not worth applying for.
(e)	Many farmers dread credit dealings with banks and mortgage companies due to past foreclosures . . .

They certainly do dread such dealings because they only have to recall what happened 15 or 20 years ago to realize just what it meant to them and their families to have hanging over their heads a bank loan which could not be paid.
It has been mentioned that the farmers of Canada are a wealthy group, that there is no need for the people of Canada as a whole to have to subsidize them, and so on. If that statement were true I would not suppose any hon. member would be arguing here for cash advances on farm-stored grain. Of course the truth of the matter is that as a group the farmers of Canada are far from being wealthy.
In the same brief presented to the federal government by the interprovincial farm union council I should like to refer to a table found on page 9 which deals with agriculture and total national income in Canada, 1945 to 1954 inclusive. I have every reason to believe that the table is backed up by authentic statistics, and in it we find that in 1945 the farmers received 11..8 per cent of the national income. In 1946 they received 13 per cent, in 1947 12-8 per cent, in 1948 13-6 per cent, and in 1949 12-8 per cent. Let us go down to the last three years for which statistics are available. In 1952 the farmers of Canada received 11-4 per cent of the national income. In 1953 they received 9-9 per cent and in 1954, 6-8 per cent.
Yet we have some hon. members still trying to convince us that the farmers of all Canada are receiving that which they justly deserve. I trust that other hon. members will get up and speak with feeling on this bill. May I say finally that I would not wish the right hon. Minister of Agriculture to feel for one moment that his harangue had one bit of influence upon my thinking, because I know the feelings of the farmers of my area. I have lived with them all my life. I know their thoughts, and I know that in the west at the present time there is a drastic shortage of money and that bank loans at 5 per cent are far from the answer to the problem.

speechtext:
As I
stated, Mr. Speaker, perhaps he was not familiar with the situation prevailing and with the work which the Saskatchewan government has done in respect of it.
Now we have the picture of the fanner being asked to accept bank loans as a measure to relieve his present cash situation. I believe that is an indignity to the farmer. It places him in an extremely difficult position, because it is only going to add to his present financial problem. The Minister of Agriculture stated that to date some $7 million had been loaned under the proposal of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, this is only another load and another debt on the western farmer. If the farmer has t&

Grain
take a year to pay back that $7 million it is going to impose a load of another $350,000 on the already harassed and debt-ridden farmer of western Canada.
Mr. Speaker, there has been a great deal of talk in the house as to what the farmers in western Canada want. The Minister of Agriculture stated that, when they were undertaking to make some proposal, bank loans seemed to be-and he gave three reasons for the provision-the quickest, the most effective and the cheapest method. I want to say that he never said it was the fairest method, and that is an important issue in this debate.
The present situation facing the farmer is the result of the lack of adequate agriculture policies by this government. I am sure that anyone who is fair-minded, after a perusal of what has taken place, will agree that the western farm organizations and the western farmers generally do not accept this legislation. Last evening the Minister of Trade and Commerce quoted what he called "hot off the griddle" submissions made by the royal commission investigating the position of agriculture in the province of Saskatchewan. As reported at page 1447 of Hansard he said: The bill was recommended by the farm leaders of the province.
I want to say that statement is not true. It is not endorsed by the farm leaders of the province. If there was any confusion in the early stages leading up to the present situation, then it could have been said that there *was not complete unanimity. However, I believe that as discussion in this house and in the country has taken place, the submissions made now by all the main agricultural organizations and farm spokesmen are to the effect that they are asking for cash advances as opposed to bank loans. When the Minister of Agriculture was speaking I asked him to read recommendation No. 14 appearing in the report of the royal commission on agriculture and rural life from which he had been quoting. I now want to quote that recommendation for the record:
That, in view of the grain producers' immediate need for cash and their present difficulty in selling farm stocks of grain, the federal government promptly establish, on an emergency basis, a system of cash advances on farm-stored grain.
In addition to that, among the people who were on the commission making this submission we have Mr. H. L. Fowler, secretary manager of federated co-operatives. Mr. Fowler now is backing cash advances for farm-stored grain. In addition there is Mr. Charles W. Gibbings, who is another member of the commission and is second vice president of the wheat pool. He is another person (Mr. McCullough (Moose Mountain).]
who is supporting cash advances. Then there is Mr. J. L. Phelps, president of the farmers of Alberta economic committee. He is supporting cash advances. In addition to that, I want to say that the resolutions which the Minister of Trade and Commerce read last evening were not necessarily final recommendations. It should be noted that in the beginning they said:
Perhaps a more workable proposal is to reestablish the Prairie Producers Interim Financing Act of 1951 on a permanent basis.
Then later on they say:
. . . the existing need could probably be met through re-enacting the Prairie Producers Interim Financing Act as permanent legislation.
They were no final conclusions whatsoever. I think I have read into the record the final recommendations which these people made, which is more to the point.
Just recently the interprovincial farm union council came to Ottawa and made their submissions to the government. In an unmistakable way they pointed out that they were asking for cash advances and not for farm loans. I read from page 15 of their brief submitted to the government:
Therefore, the interprovincial farm union council is continuing to press for adoption of its original proposal (which has been endorsed at the three wheat pool delegate meetings) that the government arranged for interest-free cash advances by the Canadian wheat board on farm-stored grain to the value of 50 per cent of the initial payment on an estimated delivery of 8 bushels per cultivated acre.
I have here also, Mr. Speaker, the Saskatchewan wheat pool's brief and I want to quote from it as follows:
The current problem of a shortage of farm cash was considered as soon as the annual meeting opened. The delegates went on record in favour of a system of cash advances against farm-stored grain to be paid out by the Canadian wheat board through elevator companies with the federal government assuming the interest on the loans involved.
I think we can all surely agree that we have a preponderance of farm leadership and farm organizations asking for cash advances at this time. I think the debate should rest on the merits or demerits of that proposal, namely whether or not the farmer is entitled to cash advances or whether he should pay interest on any alleviation of his present financial crisis.
I said at the beginning that the present farm economic problem should be laid right at the doorstep of the Liberal party. There has been confusion in respect of deliveries; there has been confusion in respect of box cars. We find that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has made a number of statements in this respect. On January 11 he said:
The weather is improving and I may say that car loadings are improving.

On January 16 he said:
The movement of box cars in the west has improved very considerably in the last two weeks, largely as a result of improved weather conditions.
On January 27 he said:
Our big problem now is not selling, but transportation. If deliveries of wheat by producers this crop year do happen to fall behind last year, it will be because rail transportation is not adequate.
Then of course the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) had some comment to make over a Winnipeg radio station. He said:
Our great problem is box cars. Of these there is a great shortage both in the United States and in Canada.
When the Minister of Agriculture was in the west the other day he made the comment to the press that there was still a shortage of box cars. He went on to say that one company making wheels for the box cars was going full blast. That certainly shows a lot of confusion, a lack of planning and a lack of knowledge on the part of this government. They are not interested in trying to get the grain off the farms into box cars and into elevators.
Then we have the comment of the transport controller, as it appeared in the Gazette of February 16. He said:
There is no shortage of box cars holding up prairie grain shipments.
It would seem that there is a lot of confusion somewhere. The net result is that this year the federal government has failed to move the grain off the farms and to pay the farmers anything for their labour. That is the crux of the whole situation. That is why the farmer has the right to demand that some cash be put in his pocket so he can pay his debts and carry on.
In my constituency I have a number of organizations. The Saskatchewan farm union district convention was held in Estevan. We had around 200 delegates. At that meeting they passed a resolution asking that cash advances be paid to farmers. In addition, at all the public meetings I held resolutions were passed, and there was unanimity in asking for cash advances as opposed to bank loans. The farmers are justified in asking for cash rather than paying interest on loans. I know that in my constituency the average young farmer who started to farm in the last seven or eight years is so short of cash that he cannot pay his fuel bills, his debts, and carry on.
I was at a large livestock feeder sale and talked to a number of young farmers. These farmers wanted to buy some cattle, put them on feed and perhaps make some money during the winter. They had grain on their farms, but simply because there was no movement of grain those young farmers
Grain
were forced to watch the big feeders come in and buy up the cattle, take them out and put them on feed lots, while they sat back and watched the auction take place without any money to buy livestock.
I remember that a year ago the Minister of Agriculture told the western farmers that if they wanted some ready cash to start raising some more hogs.

Mr. Speaker, the agricultural position today is a complete fiasco. I think we have a definite right to try to put the facts before this government. They are stubborn; they do not want to listen. Nevertheless they cannot deny the facts. They cannot deny from 1951 to 1955 agricultural income in all sections of

the country has deteriorated. It has gone down in the west more than 3 per cent over the general farm economy. It has gone down over 46 per cent in the prairie provinces. Today the western farmer's dollar stands at a parity level of about 46 per cent as compared with the purchasing power of the 1945 dollar.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, since 1945, the time of decontrol, the policies of this government have put the western farmer in an impossible financial position. His costs have gone up and up and the price of his commodities has gone down. That is why today the western farmer is in a cost-price squeeze. There is nothing the individual farmer can do, and there is nothing organized agriculture can do except to come down here and put before this government their plea that we have some kind of planning in this country by which agriculture will get a fair deal.
I noticed a press comment which stated that presumably the Minister of Trade and Commerce is indifferent or will not see the light and take into consideration that because western agriculture today is in such a financial crisis, it will eventually affect the whole Canadian economy. We have heard a lot of optimistic statements from various hon. members of the cabinet but when we ask for adequate policies we get such policies as the one we are presently discussing, namely that the farmer must be expected to go to the bank and be subjected to that indignity, and he must give a lot of information as to his financial position.
This is reminiscent of the hungry thirties. I remember the period in the thirties after we had had a Conservative government and the Liberal government was again in power. Neither of them was able to help the farmers, and I suppose the people of Saskatchewan and the prairie provinces in general were the worst hit. It got so that farmers had to sign this paper and that paper, and I remember a story concerning one farmer who when taking a load of wheat to town jumped off the wagon when he saw a piece of paper floating by and put his signature on it.
That seems to be the behaviour this government expects of the farmer in order to obtain a little bit of cash, in spite of the fact that he has farmed well and has produced wealth for this country and for hungry people abroad where we can perhaps meet the challenge of communism. The farmer is trying to provide adequately and he has done a good job. Despite the fact that he has done this he is faced with nothing short of a ridiculous and unfair policy which says in effect that after he has produced his wealth and put it in the granary he must now go and borrow on it.

I wonder how many hon. members of this house, perhaps in the year 1945, were earning $4,800 a year. I wonder too how they would react if their income today was to drop to $1,800 in terms of purchasing power, and if at the end of the year their employer said, "You are not going to get $1,800; you will have to go to the bank. We will set up a plan whereby you can go to the bank and borrow on your $1,800". That is exactly what the western farmer has to do under this policy.
The western farmer favours an orderly marketing system, he is in favour of the Canadian wheat board and he does not want speculation on food stocks. However, he does believe that this government should get busy and endeavour to sell some of the grain in storage, and that for the welfare of the whole Canadian economy we should have a policy of storing our grain somewhat akin to that which exists in the United States, where the farmer is paid as soon as he produces his grain and places it in approved storage. At that time he can obtain 90 per cent of parity for his grain. In this country we have nothing like that.

That is one thing which we in this group have been advocating since 1945 when I came into this house and I presume hon. members of this party were advocating it before then. Instead of taking an average delivery of 10 or 15 years the government should set up the principle of the normal granary, where we store in the years of plenty for years of scarcity; but no such program is forthcoming.
In closing I just want to say that this government, in spite of its numerical strength in this house; in spite of the threats of the Minister of Agriculture; in spite of what I think is the twisting of the facts of the support of this bill on the part of the Minister of Agriculture, we in this group feel the farmers of western Canada do not support bank loans. They do not want to be forced to go to the banks and pay interest on their money; in fact, they feel it is an injustice.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak for just a few minutes before the vote is taken on the second reading of this bill. I imagine most hon. members would prefer to have the vote after eight o'clock, anyway.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
However, my purpose in
rising is to urge the government to reconsider its announced refusal to send this bill after second reading to the committee on agriculture and colonization or any appropriate committee which the government might choose. Bearing in mind the dislike of the Chair and the dislike of the house for repetition at this stage of the debate, I shall not repeat the arguments for such a course. I merely make the appeal. In fact, I think one might well rest such an appeal on the arguments already made by members of this [The Acting Speaker (Mr. Applewhaite).]
group, as well as other members, particularly that of the hon. member for Acadia and the argument made this afternoon by the hon. member for Greenwood.
However, if the government feels it cannot send the bill-I am not referring to the subject matter, but to the bill itself

to committee, then serious consideration might be given to the proposition that was enunciated this afternoon by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He made an interjection during the speech made by the hon. member for Greenwood, which I took down-and I hope I took it down correctly-when he said something like this: "May I ask my hon. friend if there is any better representation of the farming community than the elected representatives from the area?"
The point the minister was making was that we do not need to send this bill to a committee to have representatives from various organizations there because, as he put it, the best representatives of the farming community-the community affected-are the elected representatives on the floor of this house. I made the suggestion, by way of a question which I put to the hon. member for Greenwood, that the minister might then consider seeking the advice of the elected representatives who he has said in his own words are the best representatives of the farming community.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Please make it snappy.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I remind the minister that the area to which he referred consists of the three prairie provinces. There are 48 constituencies in those three prairie provinces, represented in this house by 48 members. There are 14 of them from Manitoba, 17 from Saskatchewan and 17 from Alberta. Judging by the way those members have been voting on the last two amendments that have been before the house, those 48 members would vote 32 to 16 against this bill.
I submit, therefore, that on the basis of the minister's own pronouncement this afternoon he should not be calling upon the government's majority in the whole house to support a bill which he says might be subjected to the best representation from the farming community, namely the elected representatives from the area concerned. Some hon. members might say that suggestion is not put forward too seriously. I do not recall any occasion on which a committee of the house was set up on the basis of representation from a particular province or particular provinces. Therefore it might not be an appropriate precedent to establish, namely the actual appointment of a com-

Grain
mittee representing members from the three provinces named. Nevertheless, in spirit-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: An ad hoc committee.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
The hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Trainor) says it should be an ad hoc committee. Well, the members of such an ad hoc committee have already spoken in the house. They are two to one against the bill. In view of that fact it seems to me that the bill should not be allowed to pass. But if the government insists on putting it through with its majority, then it does seem to me that the case is unanswerable that it should be referred to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization.
I offer just one other objection to the bill. Although I have not sat here every minute of the debate on this legislation I have tried to follow it closely, and I believe this objection has not yet been voiced. In making this objection may I point out that one of the main reasons we from the prairie provinces oppose this legislation is that we know if it is enacted it, together with the proposal contained in Bill No. 83, will be all that the wheat farmers of western Canada will get in relation to their present crisis. We know that no matter how strong the appeals may be for further legislation, for further consideration of their plight, the fact that these two measures have been passed will put an end to any consideration by the government of the crisis in western Canada.
That is bad enough, Mr. Speaker, when it applies to the present situation. That is bad enough when that is the answer for this year, but I ask hon. members to recognize that in addition the government, through this legislation, is asking for the right by order in council to extend this bill for a second year. That means that if a year from now a situation in western Canada develops which is similar to the situation that now obtains, we will not even have the matter discussed in parliament. There will not be a summoning of a session of parliament as there should have been last fall. Of course not. But there will not even be a discussion in parliament. The matter will be decided behind the closed doors of a cabinet meeting by the passing of an order in council, and once again the farmers of western Canada will be faced with the fact that this is it so far as the government of Canada is concerned.
As one hon. member said a few days ago, 32 of us from the prairie provinces would not be committing political suicide if we felt that this legislation was popular on the prairies. We know that it is not. The fact that, despite what happened in the first vote 67509-95 J
at the resolution stage, there has been a solid opposition in the votes on the amendments that have taken place, and that there will be a solid opposition on the vote that may now take place on second reading, is in my opinion pretty conclusive evidence as to the views of the people who are affected by this legislation.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce enjoyed making his comments the other day with respect to whether my colleagues in this party were expressing the views of western agriculture, but he cannot deny the fact that the one way the people of the prairies have to express their views on national matters is through the representation they send to this house. He confirmed that this afternoon in the statement that the best representation from the farming community consists of the elected representatives here. Those elected representatives are two to one against this legislation.
Therefore I feel that it should be turned down by the house. But if the government insists on putting it through, surely the least the government can do is to have it referred to a standing committee of the house so that interested bodies may appear and further consideration may be given as to whether this is the way to deal with the matter or whether an effort should be made to find some better way.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take very long at this time. I have spoken on the bill on other occasions and have expressed my views leaving no doubt as to what I meant. When I was speaking the other day I made a statement with regard to something the Minister of Trade and Commerce had said. The effect of it was that the minister had said there were not very many people who were going to take advantage of these loans. He objected to that statement and said that I should give some proof of that fact. I informed him at that time that I would do so.
The other day I started to quote some passages from Hansard which indicate, in my judgment at least, that the minister made that implication on more than one occasion. I had put one reference on the record and then Mr. Speaker at that time, not Mr. Speaker now in the chair, stopped me and said he did not think it was a question of privilege.
I indicated, therefore, that as time went on I would put the remarks of the Minister of Trade and Commerce on Hansard to prove my point, and that I would also prove the point I had made regarding the Minister of Agriculture supporting the remarks of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I want to do this now, and it will not take more than.

Grain
a couple of minutes. As found at page 129 of Hansard of January 16, the Minister of Trade and Commerce had this to say:
A certain number of producers have found themselves in difficulty this past season, and the purpose of the guaranteed loan was to relieve those smaller producers.
I contended at that time that in referring to a certain number of producers the minister had indicated that no great number of people were intending to take advantage of the legislation. Then I want to quote another passage from the remarks of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. As found near the top of page 129 he said:
Apart from that-
He was referring to the storage question, -it did not seem to me that there was any particular burden on the farmer through this condition of plenty.
Again I say, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Trade and Commerce pointed out that because of the surplus situation there was no unnecessary burden on the farmers, and that very few would take advantage of this legislation. To make it more definite, I want to put on Hansard what the Minister of Trade and Commerce is reported as having said in Calgary. These are his words, and without doubt I think they will convince the house that the minister did not have in mind that very many people would take advantage of the legislation. As found in the Calgary Herald of November 28, 1955, the minister is reported as saying:
It is my hope and belief that comparatively limited use will be made of the lending facilities, that most farmers are either in a position to carry on without borrowing or are in a position to finance in the ordinary way.
Then the Minister of Agriculture said just today in his speech, and I wrote down his words at the time he uttered them, that a very small percentage of the farmers will go to the banks for these loans. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, I did not misquote the Minister of Trade and Commerce. What I said was perfectly true and I still stand by what I said the other day with respect to what the minister had said.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the minister would elaborate on the word "interim". It would seem to me that since the act provides that by order in council it can be extended to a year from now there should be some indication as to what the minister has in mind by the reference "interim".

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the purpose of the word interim is to indicate that it is not the intention of the act to take care of all the requirements of the producer for a year. It is to take care of a producer in the interim from the beginning of the crop year until he is able to deliver wheat or other grain in an amount that is current in a normal year.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
But, Mr. Chairman, since provision is made for the legislation to be extended by order in council, I think that would suggest in the minds of those who were drafting it that it probably will be applicable next year. With such large sections of the west where farmers have been able to deliver only one bushel per acre up until this time,
Grain
and with the picture as serious as it is, IT would think there should be some indication; as to whether or not the farmers are going to be able to find some other ways and means of realizing on the sizeable stocks of grain which are in hand but which cannot be sold.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, no matter what the title suggests to my hon. friend it is in fact an interim loan. The farmer starts repaying it as soon as he delivers any grain and over a period of time the loan is bound to diminish, providing the farmer is able to market his grain.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:

It was not possible to conclude that, and it is not possible to conclude the matter in time for this legislation. I hope I shall be able to do so before another bill of similar import may come forward. I can assure my hon. friend that so far as we are concerned there is no objection to credit unions. maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.

speechtext:
I notice that paragraph (d) of subclause 1 of clause 3 refers to the rate of interest charged by the bank on the loan not exceeding 5 per cent. In other words the guarantee would apply if the rate of interest charged by the bank on the loan did not exceed 5 per cent per annum simple interest. This would indicate a maximum figure. Can the minister inform the committee if the banks have handled any of these loans at less than 5 per cent interest?
The reason I ask the question is that it seems to me the guarantee supplied in this case is very much the same as when a borrower goes to the bank, asks for $1,500, is questioned as to his security and presents $1,500 in Dominion of Canada bonds. Under circumstances of that kind I am quite sure that any bank manager would be prepared to lend at a rate less than 5 per cent. I have been told that there may be problems of collection involved in this instance which are a little different from just having to cash bonds, but I am quite sure that if the banks had certain problems of collection they would in

the ordinary course of events add their collection charges to the amount which they would be attempting to collect. Perhaps the minister might answer first if there have been any loans at less than 5 per cent and, second, just what type of negotiations took place with the chartered banks leading up to the rate fixed under this legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
If a borrower were prepared to put up $1,500 in government bonds he would not make use of this legislation. He would conduct his own negotiations with the bank. Of course the bank does not need $1,500 in government bonds plus the government guarantee. I dare say if they had both they might give him quite a good rate. This legislation is concerned with the borrower whose only security is the wheat on his farm, and as far as I know the rate is 5 per cent.
These are small loans. The average is about $800, and the period of time would not be over six months. Probably it would not be as much as that. Therefore the total amount collected by the bank would be $20 per loan, and for that sum the bank has to go to the expense of making and collecting the loan. There is no such thing as adding collection charges, so my hon. friend need not worry about that.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I am satisfied with the explanation respecting no collection charges, but I do not think the minister should try to confuse me by telling me that if a man had $1,500 in bonds he would not be going to the bank to borrow under this legislation. I realize that. What I am saying is that the guarantee by the government to the bank is just as good security as the $1,500 in bonds that he might have taken to the bank if he had them. maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.

a bank manager as to which he would rather have as security, $1,500 in government bonds or alternatively $1,500 in respect of which the government has given a 20 per cent guarantee, I think he would certainly choose the former.
