maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we in this group have continued to say that under the legislation before us the banks in fact are taking no risk at all and that the 10 per cent of the

Grain
aggregate that is guaranteed could not possibly under any circumstances be reached. I can therefore agree with those who say that, with such a complete guarantee by the federal government, the banks should certainly be able to do better than to put out their money at the rather high rate of 5 per cent.
In answer to a question by the hon. member for Prince Albert, the minister has just placed on record the experience of the government in connection with a guarantee on somewhat similar lines in 1951. It shows that on aggregate loans of $625,000, to date the loss to the treasury has been $13,880. I am sure the minister hopes that some of the money still owing may yet be collected, and that what has been a loss to date of approximately 2 per cent may be still further reduced. I would think the 2 per cent loss is probably higher than that which is likely to be experienced under this act.
The 1951 legislation was enacted to deal with a situation that was different in many respects. Today we are dealing with a situation where the farmers have grain of high grade, in excellent condition and in good storage. It is the grain itself that is the guarantee that the bank loan will be paid. But in 1951, when marketing conditions were better, it was not a question of a farmer with grain finding it difficult to get his grain to market. The situation was that owing to adverse weather conditions in the fall of 1951, thousands of farmers had not been able to harvest their crop and the crop itself in an unthreshed condition was out under the snow. Because the farmers had no grain to market, the government decided to guarantee a loan. In this legislation the loan is against grain in storage. But in the legislation of 1951 the security was the crop and the crop was defined as follows:
(e) "crop" means a crop of grain of any kind, as well before as after severance from the soil, harvesting or threshing thereof, and includes grain of any kind.
The grain could not only be under the snow in a swath condition where there was perhaps a reasonably good chance of harvesting it in the spring, but the grain could be under the snow in a standing condition so it was difficult to say what the possibility might be of harvesting the grain the next spring.
Still, with respect to this legislation, there is a high interest rate of 5 per cent. The farmer is obliged to surrender his permit book. He is giving the banks, I suggest, full security. I wonder what the right of the farmer is under this act. Is the farmer with grain undelivered, with his permit book uncommitted as defined in this legislation, in
fact entitled to a loan? I do not think so. I still believe it is at the discretion of the banker whether the loan is in fact made. Because of the fact that we object to this extremely high rate of interest, Mr. Chairman, we oppose this particular clause.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I am quite willing to assume that there will be no loss to the banks and I am quite willing to assume that the loss-if there is a loss-to the government will be extremely small. Nevertheless, it costs money to carry on a banking business. It costs money to make small loans. My hon. friend has before the house at the present time an amendment to the Small Loans Act, and it covers loans of about the same amount as these loans. What interest rate did he provide for there?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, they are not at all comparable. The purpose of the legislation which I proposed to the house was to reduce the interest rate that borrowers would be obliged to pay when they obtained loans under the Small Loans Act. The borrower who is asking for a loan from a small loan company has already been paid his wages-* at least we assume that-or if he has a product to sell, he has been able to sell it. But the fact is that the prairie producer, while he has perhaps one of the best crops in history, has not been able to deliver it.
Because the wheat board and the government, who have the sole responsibility of marketing that grain, have been unable to take delivery of a substantial part of the grain to date, we feel the government has some responsibility. It is probably more just that a person, in obtaining a loan after he has received his wages, should pay an interest rate even though it is in excess of 5 per cent, than it is that a person be forced to pay 5 per cent interest because of the failure, through government policy, to take delivery of that grain.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
We in this group have already stated that we think the interest rate is too high. Inasmuch as apparently the losses are guaranteed by the government, there is therefore no real danger of the banks suffering any loss. But what I am interested in is this. How far must the banks go in collecting the money that is owed to them before the government will pay up any losses they may have suffered? For instance, if when the grain has been delivered there is still a certain amount of money owing to the banks, can the banks then claim that they have suffered loss or must they take other measures in order to try to collect the money that is owing to them, such as foreclosing on chattels or any other assets?

Grain

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I believe that matter is covered by the regulations. The bank is obliged to make a reasonable effort to collect the money. I think there is a recovery section in it:
The bank shall notwithstanding full settlement of its claim of loss as a result of the guarantee loan act on behalf of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to collect amounts outstanding in respect of the loan and for such purpose shall take such reasonable steps as the said minister may deem necessary and shall realize upon any security held by it such amounts as may be collected or realized by it to be remitted to the said minister at the end of each month, commencing with the first day of November, 1952.
That is a regulation from the 1951 legislation, but that will be covered by the regulations in this case.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: The reason I asked that question is this. When we were considering the housing legislation the representatives of the banks stated that they did not like to go into the mortgage business because they did not want to be obliged to foreclose. maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: If the wheat does not pay up the loss, as far as the bankers are concerned they are through?

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the clause in regard to the maximum rate of interest needs some further clarification. I think it will shock a great many people to learn that a loan guaranteed by the government of Canada should call for a rate as high as 5 per cent. It is quite true that there are limitations on the amount of the loan. There are limitations imposed by this section and there are limitations imposed by the next following section. Therefore it cannot be said that it is a complete, unconditional guarantee of the loans by the government of Canada. But even taking account of that fact, the rate of interest seems high in relation to the kind of security this bill authorizes.
Seeing that this must have been the subject of conferences with the banks before the

lending began as of October 1, I ask the minister whether this subject of the rate of interest was seriously discussed, and whether the government did press for a lower rate of interest on these bank loans, in view of the extent of the government guarantee?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance, of course, deals with the banks, and discussions about the rate of interest were carried on by the Minister of Finance. The government has many guaranteed loans and I do not know that 5 per cent has ever been considered a high interest rate. The Farm Improvement Loans Act is the same and the National Housing Act is a bit higher. If my hon. friend says that 5 per cent for a loan averaging $800 is an excessive rate, he is expressing his own opinion; he certainly is not expressing mine.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I think the minister is only adding confusion to the situation. He is talking about certain loans made by government boards under certain acts to individual borrowers. That is not the situation under this bill at all. This is a question of banks lending to individual borrowers, and receiving at the same time a government guarantee. I did not use the expression "excessive interest rate" as the minister has. But I do wish to express the opinion that I think it will shock a great many people to learn that a loan that is guaranteed by the Bank of Canada still must bear a 5 per cent rate. It will shock many people to learn that that should be so. A great many people in this country would like to lend money, receiving on it a government guarantee, for a lesser rate than 5 per cent. If there were any sense to this, I think the minister should say so rather than introduce a lot of confusing references to situations which are not at all parallel to this in any sense.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the Farm Improvement Loans Act is exactly the same as this. It provides that a borrower borrows from a bank under a government guarantee. It has been in effect for several years, and the rate is 5 per cent.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: It is too much.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: A more parallel act is the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act under which the fisherman borrows from a bank under a government guarantee at an interest rate of 5 per cent. It is the same class of loan.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Can the minister tell us what was the amount of loss under the Farm Improvement Loans Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
It is not in the
Department of Trade and Commerce.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: The Canadian Farm Loan Act is certainly not comparable.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I said "Farm Improvement Loans Act".

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Certainly not the Canadian Farm Loan Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I should like to say a word about the time period for which these loans are guaranteed. The bill says loans made between November 15, 1955 and June 1, 1956. Here we are in February, and parliament is now going to guarantee loans which have been made as far back as November 15, I suppose under the assurance of the government that it would cause parliament to pass the necessary regulation. It is that kind of attitude of the government toward parliament which leads me to ask the minister whether the date was not intended to be November 5, which was the date on which the announcement was made and which, as students of history will recall, is Guy Fawkes day, and the anniversary of the gunpowder plot to blow up parliament. I thought the minister had some sense of poetic justice in what he was doing in making his announcement on Guy Fawkes day. Perhaps he would like to amend this section and have the date run from November 5 to June 1.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if I had the same finicky view of the situation as my hon. friend has I would probably have decided to wait until parliament had met and this lengthy debate was over, and the farmers would only now be able to get loans instead of getting them last November. I daresay it helped.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Possibly the minister can explain whether or not an order in council was passed to cover the guarantees that had been made from the date when the banks were promised this guarantee back on November 5 until the date that parliament did meet. Is that the basis upon which the guarantee was carried into effect?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman,, there was no order in council. There were letters from the Minister of Finance to the banks which were tabled in the house. I am quite sure my hon. friend has read them. I do not know why he asked the question.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, that is not quite the answer; that is no answer at all. The Minister of Finance has no power outside of parliament or under an order of council under the prerogative right of the crown.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
No power to write a letter?
Grain

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Oh, now, we have arrived at the point where a minister can write a letter and make a guarantee on behalf of the government of Canada without an order in council. That is a most interesting thing. That is a new principle of government.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: The Minister of Finance made no guarantee. He wrote a letter to say that when the house convened he would introduce legislation to guarantee the loans from a certain period, which I think was November 15. That was the letter to the banks. The banks did not even wait. They decided they would lend on the basis of that letter, believing that the Minister of Finance would introduce the bill as he had promised, which has been done.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Has that letter been
tabled?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: That is the one that was tabled?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: The one in question; I see.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
My hon. friends laugh. Because of the delay in tabling them it makes one suspicious, any time any matter arises, that they have not been tabled. I want to ask some questions in regard to directions to the banks. One of the complaints that I have had from quite a number of farmers is that qualified farmers are denied loans under the terms of the legislation. It all seems to depend on the location of the bank or the attitude of the individual banker.
What instructions have been given to the banks in regard to this question? In certain places farmers have been denied loans with all types of excuses. One excuse has been, well, you really do not need the money at the present time because you are going to make payments on account of certain debts that you owe. That excuse has been used on a number of occasions. Farmers believe that they are entitled to this assistance because after all one of the major reasons for it was to relieve the monetary situation among the farmers, and also, I would think, to be of assistance to the creditors in the area in which those farmers live in order to meet the current expenses of farming.
What instructions have been given to the banks? I asked the other day whether the government had any record of how many applications were turned down by the various chartered banks. The reply I received was that the government had no such information. I feel that if instructions have not

Grain
been given to the banks, instructions should certainly go out now from the Minister of Finance to the various banks requesting them to grant the necessary loans, since the banks are guaranteed against any possibility of loss. Will the minister say-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, there are only two criteria that must be insisted on. One is, has the farmer the grain? In other words if he has 2,000 bushels of wheat he is entitled to borrow on a thousand bushels. The other is, is it pledged under section 88 to some other bank? If it is not, or if it is pledged under section 88 to the same bank and there is room for the loan, he is entitled to the loan. Those are the only two criteria.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Is there not another under section 3(e)? If the farmer had sold his 2-bushel quota would not the amount of that be deducted from the $1,500?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Yes. This is supposed to put the farmer who has delivered no grain in cash until he has delivered his grain, and if he has delivered part of his grain that is counted against the loan and he is only entitled to borrow the $1,500 less the value of the grain that he has delivered.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: What if the farmer has only delivered 2 bushels per acre-the normal delivery is 8-surely the farmer should be able to borrow something; but if he had 800 acres at 2 bushels that would be 1,600 and that would mean he would not be able to borrow a cent. Yet he would have 6 bushels to the acre left on which he should be able to borrow.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: If he had 3,000 bushels he could borrow $1,500, I suppose, and if he has delivered 500 bushels that is taken off; but this legislation was never intended for a man who has 800,000 bushels of grain or anything like that.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
How much did
you say?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Eight hundred.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: What is a million bushels?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
This is for the
small farmer, the three-quarter section farmer who would be expected to produce about 3,000 bushels of grain. That is the man this legislation was designed for. My hon. friend likes to refer to his own position, but I venture to suggest a bank manager does not ask him for any guarantee when he goes in to borrow.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: It has been argued constantly that the risk involved does not warrant the high interest rate of 5 per cent, and the minister referred to the experience in 1951 and the small loss taken, which seems to fairly well justify that belief. [DOT] I wonder if the minister could tell us of the $13,000 that did go into default in the 1951 experience; how many of those loans went into default because of misrepresentations made by producers as to the amount of grain they gave as security to the bank?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: We would not know that. These loans are put out by chartered banks. I suppose they do their best to collect, but whether there is misrepresentation or misfortune or whatever cause we would not know.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the minister has stated that this legislation is aimed at assisting the small farmer providing he can meet the qualifications of section 3. The qualification of section 3(c) is that the bank manager has scrutinized and checked the application for the loan with the care required of him by the bank in thg conduct of its ordinary business.
I suppose all bank managers are charged with the responsibility of making money and not losing any; therefore the bank manager would not give the loan to anyone who is in any way a poor risk. He would not give it to the small farmer who is in need of it by virtue of this qualification which is stated in the act. Is that not correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
All I can say is
that up to the end of last year he had already given it to 8,000 farmers, and I am sure he has given it to a great many more since that time.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Has the minister any information as to the number of farmers who have applied?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Not the slightest.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: It is listed on the application for the loan which the Minister of Finance has. Could the minister get that information? Surely it must be part of the information which the Minister of Finance has.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: It is not available in Ottawa.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Would the minister care to state at just what price per bushel this grain which is to be hypothecated for loans is to be held?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: It is the initial price of the grade.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: What is that, $1.40?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: It depends on the grade.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I should like to ask another question with regard to the security. Since all the loans are going to be entered in the farmer's permit book, the security upon which the loan is made is not merely the grain which the farmer has on hand at this time but all the grain which he may have in years to come. Is that true or is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Yes, that is true.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I think the point has been well made that there has been very little risk involved in these bank loans. The hon. members who have spoken have indicated that there has been very little loss under the 1951 legislation, and I expect there will be very little loss under this legislation. This afternoon the minister indicated that to date some $7 million had been loaned under the present proposed legislation. Calculating that at 5 per cent interest, if it runs for a year there will be an additional debt of $350,000 on the farmers' backs.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: It does not run for a year.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
But
certainly it may very well run for a year.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: No, sir.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Consequently I say it smacks of discrimination, simply because when we consider other legislation proposed by this government to help various companies in this country at around 3 or 3,j per cent interest, one can readily understand our disgust. The farmer is already bankrupt because of this government's policy.
I take exception to this because as the minister has said, it is an ironclad guarantee by the government of up to 15 per cent of the aggregate loss the banks can have. I think all hon. members will agree that at the outside the loss will be only about 2 per cent, and when it is considered that this legislation is supposed to help the small farmer in general one can agree with what has been said by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort and the hon. member for Kindersley and others who have said that the farmer in many cases is not going to receive any assistance under this legislation.
If for example the farmer has his grain hypothecated to taxes, to the storekeeper, the oil merchant and to others, and if he has made a delivery under the quota, then of course his chances of getting a loan are very remote.
Grain
When one considers that the farmer is hard pressed at the present time I think the government should have given fair consideration to this. At least when it is prepared to back it with the Canadian taxpayer's money so the banks cannot possibly experience the loss contemplated of 15 per cent of the aggregate, then I think we should have at least found this government ready to compromise on this and ready to reduce the interest to approximately 3 per cent, which it was ready to give big companies in this country in relation to credit and advances.
I think there are certain friends of this government, but the farmers of western Canada are not among them. The friends of the government appear to be the vested interests, corporations, and big people who can do something for themselves. Very little if any consideration is given to the little fellow and, I refer particularly to the farmers of western Canada.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: May I ask the minister an additional question? Supposing he accepted the suggestion which has just been made, how much does he estimate it would cost the treasury of Canada, if anything?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: What was the suggestion just made?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: The suggestion was made that the interest rate be reduced to 3 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Well, I suppose if the banks charged 5 per cent and we charged the farmer 3 per cent someone would have to pay the other 2 per cent. My hon. friend has a pencil there; he can figure it out.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Not necessarily; the banks could be persuaded to charge 3 per cent.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, a few minutes ago when the interest rate was under discussion the Minister of Trade and Commerce tried to make the point that 5 per cent was the rate charged in certain other acts providing for government-guaranteed loans. He referred in particular to the Farm Improvement Loans Act and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. It seems to me that there is a very fundamental difference between loans sought under those acts and the loans provided for under this legislation, a fundamental difference which we do not as yet seem to have been able to get across to the minister.
When a farmer seeks a loan under the Farm Improvement Loans Act he is seeking money to improve his property or to purchase machinery, knowing that he will have to repay that loan-and intending to do so-out of future earnings. But in this case the farmer is put in the position where he has to seek

Grain
a loan in respect of wages he has already earned but has not been able to draw. It is because of that fundamental difference that we think there should be cash advances rather than loans. In other words, we think that there should be no interest at all. We contend that the minister's attempt to make a comparison is invalid.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am certain that my hon. friend is so indoctrinated with the idea of collective farms, government-owned farms, that he talks about the farmer's production as labour. The farmer is an entrepreneur, he is an owner. His rewards come from the product he sells. The farmer does not work for a wage unless he is a hired man. On the collective farms in the old country wages are paid to the farmer and the state owns the land. The state takes the profits from the farm and stands the risks. But here we have ownership of the land by a private individual. The owner of the land cultivates his farm, markets his product and takes whatever comes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Just because the minister and I both happened to mention some fisheries legislation is no reason why he should produce a red herring. As a matter of fact, he knows that the inference which he has just attempted to draw is quite unfair and quite unrealistic.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
No, you are a
socialist.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
The fact of the matter is that in this country under a system which we in this group thoroughly approve, namely, orderly marketing through the wheat board, the only way in which a farmer-call him an owner if you will-can get a return for his year's work is to be able to market his product. You are indulging in semantics if you call him a labourer or wage earner because he collects his wages at the end of the year. The fact of the matter is that it is the inadequacy of the government's policy which makes it impossible for him to get that return.
I come back to the point which I made when I rose before. What the farmer will be seeking under this legislation, what he is forced by the government to apply for, is a portion of what he has already earned. That is totally different from trying to borrow something against future earnings. That being the case, there should not be any interest in this bill at all.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I can see that we all have different opinions about interest rates and also about the effectiveness of the security. Listening to the hon.
[Mr. Knowles.)
member for Winnipeg South deal with the question of interest it seemed to me that the Minister of Trade and Commerce or the Minister of Finance owes this house an outline of the negotiations which took place with the banks, not just a tabling of correspondence. I think we are entitled to know if the officials of the department sat down with the representatives of the banks to determine what would be an equitable interest rate, and whether there were any representations on the part of the treasury that 5 per cent was too high, that the banks could make a reasonable profit at 3J per cent. Did they simply accept the proposition by the banks as being the only one under which they would carry out their obligations? I think we are entitled to an explanation and to know exactly what took place.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has suggested that there should be some variation in the interest rates on loans provided for fishermen and those provided for farmers.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I did not say any such thing. I made a comparison between the farmer borrowing under one act and the farmer borrowing under another act. It was the minister who brought in the fish.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
That is what I want to speak about. I believe the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre mentioned fish as well. The fishermen in the riding which I represent are asking for loans this year for the first time, and I can assure you that they have not a year's supply of fish in storage. The reason they are asking for these loans is that last year was a bad year. If they had had two, three or four productive years they would be the last people in the world to ask anyone for assistance of any kind. The fact is that they have had two and three and in some cases four years of scarcity, and I mean scarcity.
During the past year legislation was passed in this house to provide them with the same facilities we are giving the western farmers. I can assure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that the fishermen who are taking advantage of this legislation are men who have been without income for two or three years. I think it is a most unfair comparison when you take one who has had four or five bountiful years and whose next year's bread and butter is in storage.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Perhaps I might state to the committee, and I think hon. members will agree, it having been understood that there was a comparison made between fishing legislation and farming legislation,

and that comparison having been answered, while I am not ruling comparisons out of order I think I should rule out of order debate as to the merits or needs of fishermen.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: On a question of privilege, I wish to make it perfectly clear that I referred to the fisheries act only to pick up what the minister had said, but when I made the comparison which I sought to make I made it between the farmer applying under the Farm Improvement Loans Act and the farmer applying under this bill. I deliberately and distinctly avoided making any other comparison, because if it were in order I would support the kind of appeal the hon. member for Charlotte is making on behalf of the fishermen.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I was under the impression that in his statement the hon. member said there should be a difference in the interest rate on loans to western farmers and on loans to fishermen, that the western farmer should have a lower rate. I may have misunderstood the hon'. member.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I invite my hon. friend to go with me to the Hansard office and I am sure it will be found that I said no such thing.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have listened to this debate for a long time and have not taken any part in it, but apparently some hon. members do not understand the farmer's position as a producer. He is a little different from the industrial worker. The mere fact that he owns his farm does not make so much difference, 1 should think. The difference is this. The industrial worker sells his labour to somebody who wants to buy it-or, more correctly, his labour power. He gets paid for that. What he produces belongs to the person who bought his labour. The farmer does not sell his labour power or his labour directly to anybody. He turns that labour into some kind of agricultural commodity, into oats, wheat, beef or pork or whatever he may be producing. The moment he has produced that, he has to find a buyer and he is actually in the same position as the industrial worker.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: No, he is not.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: You settle that for yourself. He is in the same position as the industrial worker who cannot find a buyer for his labour. The farmer on the prairies today who has wheat on his farm and cannot find a buyer is like the unemployed worker. He is in exactly the same position.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
There is a remarkable difference. The farmer who cannot
Grain
market his wheat still has his wheat. The unemployed worker has no income; he has only outgo.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: One works for nothing, and the other sits around for nothing.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: The farmer who has his wheat markets it in a reasonable time, it is true, and the industrial worker who cannot find a sale for his labour has his labour power, but that too has to be sold or used every day in order to be of any value to him. There is very little difference.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
There is a lot of
difference.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: If the farmer cannot find a market for his product, as I said before, he is in the same position as the worker who is unemployed. As a matter of fact, what you are doing now is providing some sort of unemployment insurance for the farmer.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: The farmer who cannot sell his wheat at least has his wheat. Suppose we take a year when the farmer cannot sell his wheat. At the end of the year he has the year's production of wheat. If a worker is unemployed for a year, he has nothing at the end of the year.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: In view of the demonstration by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway of the complete socialism of the wheat grower in this country, how can the minister maintain that the wheat farmer is in the position of an independent entrepreneur?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I suppose the most independent man is the grower of Durum wheat or the grower of flax. They can sell those whenever they like. Yet we have more complaints from those people than from anyone else. They are free agents, but they are not happy about it.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: In other words, there is no wheat board in their case.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Some of us have been saying that the position of the farmer is identical with the position of the wage earner who would have to borrow his wages at the end of the month. The minister says that is just some evidence that the C.C.F. believe in socializing the farmer.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Does the C.C.F.
not believe in socialism?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Not socializing farmers; absolutely not.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Just everybody else.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
The minister has stated that the farmer is an entrepreneur, that the

Grain
farmer is a capitalist and that he is not a wage earner. We cannot demonstrate that he is a wage earner, because he is not getting any wages. The minister cannot demonstrate that the farmer is an entrepreneur when he is not getting any return on his capital investment. He has a capital investment and he does a good deal of work, but he gets nothing for it. I think the definition of a capitalist is somebody who gets a return on his capital.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Oh.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: But we have the minister-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: You will be driving a wedge between the Conservatives and the C.C.F. if you are not careful.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I have in my hands some figures on the amount of return a farmer gets on his capital invested under the kind of system the minister is talking about.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I suggest that there is nothing in this that has anything to do with the clause under discussion.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I was about to raise that point myself. The position in which the farmer finds himself today, and whether or not he should be called upon to pay a certain rate of interest, undoubtedly come under this particular clause; but if we get too far afield into the very broad principles of whether a farmer is a capitalist or a wage earner or whether or not the C.C.F. believe in socialism, we are getting too far from the subject. The hon. member for Assiniboia might point his remarks to the clause under discussion.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: It is obvious that the Liberals do not believe in liberalism.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: It would be very difficult for a farmer or anyone else to pay interest when he is getting no interest on his investment. The figures I have show how impossible it is for farmers to pay a higher interest charge than they have been paying in recent times.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I can assure my hon. friend that, if he has figures, he has put them on Hansard at least four times in the last six weeks.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
That is another inaccurate statement of the minister. I have not yet mentioned these figures. He says I have put them on Hansard four times, and he does not know what the figures are. He has no idea what I am going to say, but he is so impatient with parliament and so impatient with discussion that he cannot wait until a member has finished his sentence before he gets up and interrupts with a lot of inaccurate statements.

As far as I know, these particular figures have not yet been placed on the record of this house by any other member.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: What are you reading from?

The interprovincial farm union council presentation to the cabinet. The figures are all taken from the dominion bureau of statistics and no doubt have been issued under the authority of the minister or, if they were not, there is another source, the Manitoba government's submission to the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects, another body set up by this government. In any case the Liberal party and this government are very closely associated with these statistics, even though I cannot tell at a quick glance whether they were issued by the dominion bureau of statistics.
They are to be found on page 8 of that submission. It is called "Table VII" and the heading is "Gross and Net Income, Operating Expenses, Total Debt and Per Cent Returns to Capital for Farms in Manitoba". You could not blame any low rate of return in Manitoba for anything a socialist provincial government might be doing, because the people out there have a provincial Liberal government as well as a federal Liberal government. In 1954 for each dollar of capital invested in Manitoba the farmers received a return of .001 per cent, which I suggest shows that the farmer, under the legislation and under the policy of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, is not a capitalist at all, because he gets zero return on his investment.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: What is the comparable figure for Saskatchewan under the socialist government?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
While the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was speaking, some exception was taken to his suggestion that the farmer is in a position where he can sell his wheat to the wheat board, and to the wheat board only. We should not lose sight of the fact that twice during the last century farmers were prevented from selling their wheat in the open market in order to keep the price down, and they were forced to sell through the wheat board.
I am not complaining about that. I am all for it, but we must not ignore that fact. We cannot sell our wheat any place else. I wish the minister would admit the correctness of the information he gives us regarding what has happened in the case of farmers in other countries, as found in the Wheat Review for December, published by the authority of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, in which he refers to what is being done for

"the wheat farmers in the Argentine, in Australia, France and elsewhere in Europe.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: We have heard that a hundred times.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: You have not heard this at all. What the hon. member for Qu'Appelle says is typical, that they have heard all this many times when they have never heard it at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: You gave us all that.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I wish the Minister of Trade and Commerce would merely go as far as his colleague, the Minister of Finance, and admit that the jam we are in now has been brought about partly because of policies that have been formulated and carried out in other countries. I realize that when we are exporting such a large percentage of our production we are not in the same position as the United States, but I think that at some point the minister should admit that Canadian farmers have no place to sell their wheat except to his wheat board. He should admit that farmers' marketings for the period from August 1 last until February 8 have dropped from 138 million bushels to 115 million bushels, and that money is scarce.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, up to this moment I had thought that this was a rather model committee of the whole. The questions that have been addressed to the government have been pointed and on the clauses concerned. The opinions expressed have been opinions with respect to the clauses concerned. But my hon. friend is now saying in a different form arguments he has used at least twice, if not three times, on the motion for second reading and the amendments thereto. Remarks of that kind are out of order in committee of the whole, and while I appreciate the fact that he may have quoted me in his last remarks I suggest that he should direct his remarks to the particular clause under discussion.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Trade and Commerce stated that the rate of interest under the bill was no higher than the rate of interest under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. That is true. It is also no higher than the rate of interest under the Veterans Business and Professional Loans Act. But the minister must be aware of the fact that when both these measures were before the house a number of members on this side of the house and I think some of the members on the other side of the house objected when we were in committee to a rate of 5 per cent being charged when the loans were being
Grain
guaranteed by the government. I think members on all sides of the house felt that when loans were guaranteed by the government the chartered banks should be able to make them at less than 5 per cent.
That is why some of us wonder whether or not the government endeavoured to get the chartered banks to make loans at a lower rate than 5 per cent where the loans are guaranteed by the government. It may be argued that the banks perhaps said they were not going to make loans at less than that rate. On the other hand, the government is of course in a position where it can bring pressure upon the chartered banks to make loans at less than 5 per cent. If the government wish to do so they have the power to tell the chartered banks, "You will have to make loans at less than 5 per cent or we will have to take action to make loans available at that rate ourselves."
All that would be necessary would be for the government to say to the chartered banks, "Now, if you do not make loans at less than 5 per cent we will get the money from the Bank of Canada; then we will increase the cash reserve requirements of the chartered banks so you cannot use that money issued by the Bank of Canada for the purpose of expanding credit." If that were drawn to the attention of the chartered banks I believe they would probably think twice before they would refuse a request by the government to make loans at less than 5 per cent.
Remember that some years ago we had Mr. Towers before the banking committee, and he told us that he estimated it cost the banks approximately 3 per cent to create money. If it costs the banks 3 per cent to create money, then surely on loans guaranteed by the government they should be prepared to make loans at cost. As has already been pointed out, they are making loans at cost, if 3 per cent is the cost, to the wheat board, and they are making loans to the wheat pools at approximately 3f per cent, just three-quarters of one per cent above their cost as estimated by the former governor of the Bank of Canada. In view of that fact I think it would be interesting to know whether or not the government did attempt to get the banks to make loans at a lower rate than 5 per cent.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, since I asked the same question as the last speaker some time ago I want to say that I dissociate myself entirely from any suggestion that the banks should be forced to deal in any manner whatsoever. In my view whatever should have been done in this case should have been done by open negotiation and mutual agreement. Am I to take it

Grain
from the silence of both the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Finance that no round table discussions were held and no case was put forward for the farmers to see if a lower rate of interest could not be obtained in connection with these loans?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Of course not, Mr. Chairman.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: We are glad to have you answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: There were negotiations and conversations over several days with respect to all the terms of the loans that might be made. Opinions were expressed about the rate of interest and whether it should be lower or higher, and as a result of those discussions the conclusion reached is in this bill.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I have been
wondering about the interest rate. It occurs to me that if the government is assuming the ultimate responsibility for these loans now at 5 per cent, the government would be in no worse financial position if they were to borrow the money from the banks at the reduced rates at which governments can borrow from the banks and provide the wheat board with those funds for loans at a recoverable rate of interest, which would restore to the treasury all the funds they would be advancing and at the same time provide loans at a rate of interest much more favourable to the farmers. I understand that the legislation is intended to benefit the farmers, and it seems to me that consideration might have been taken into account by the government.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I think I can answer that. At the moment the wheat board loan amounts to approximately $450 million. One piece of paper covers the loan of $450 million. I think my hon. friend will realize there is a good deal of work involved in putting any loan through and that, with the average loan under this legislation being about $800 and the average period being six months, it might be a little more costly to make small loans than a big loan.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Can the Minister of Finance tell me whether he considers that the treasury would have been in an adverse position if they had followed the course I suggested?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
What the Minister of Trade and Commerce is really saying is that it is a question of the service charge being different

with regard to the two types of loans. I wonder whether any figure has been worked out as to just what is the cost of servicing these individual loans, and I should like to ask whether the service charge could not be assessed against the borrower rather than the interest charge.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: The service charge is assessed against the borrower through the interest rate. I do not think the borrower would want to owe some indefinite service charge in addition to the interest rate.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Would it not be possible to separate the two? Presumably the interest rate is the profit for the banker in addition to the service charge for his services. Would it not be possible to separate the two so the farmer would merely pay the service charge on the loan?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I suppose anything is possible.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I should like to ask the Minister of Finance again whether he would agree that the government would be assuming no greater risk of loss of public funds if they had proceeded on the course of borrowing the money themselves from the banks at the rates which are available for government borrowing and had advanced the money at the same rate, with a slight addition for carrying charges, to the farmers through the wheat board. Would their risks have been any greater, and would there have been any loss to the treasury by following that course?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, we do not normally go into that business, although my hon. friend may very well say if his party were in office they would do so. However, I do not recall an occasion in the past when a transaction of the nature he has mentioned has been undertaken. Perhaps I am wrong in that regard. But our guarantee is a guarantee of a certain percentage of losses. It is not a guarantee of all losses. As I take it, my hon. friend's description of what he was going to do would mean that we would suffer all the losses that might occur.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman. But I imagine that the government have statistical data upon which they base their guarantee of a percentage of the losses. From past experience they knew that the losses were not likely to exceed that amount. In fact I think they are fairly sure that they are not going to approach that percentage. I cannot see that there would be any more likelihood of the farmers being

unable to repay the loans if they came from the government than there would be if they came from the banks.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Shall the clause carry?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Carried.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman. I wonder whether either the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Trade and Commerce discussed with the various elevator companies whether or not the elevator companies might be prepared to make such loans through their own facilities?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: The matter has been discussed. It was certainly discussed with them when the 1951 legislation was being considered. I discussed it with several of them when the question of assistance last autumn was being considered. Certainly no responsible elevator owner wants to be an intermediary in a matter of this kind.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: The information I was given-* it is now two or three years ago-along with some of my colleagues is that the Saskatchewan wheat pool at the time of the 1951 legislation made an offer to the government of the use of its facilities in making such advances to farmers. If my memory serves me correctly they made an offer to provide advances to farmers for an aggregate guarantee of 2J per cent. I am wondering whether this time the minister received any offer from any of the elevator companies suggesting that they would be prepared to make the advances.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I think that is correct, Mr. Chairman. I think the Saskatchewan wheat pool undertook to handle the loans under a government guarantee. I am certain that the interest rate was not going to be 2J per cent. That might have been the service charge by the elevator company, with the interest rate in addition. That was on the understanding that the government was to provide the funds. But it was the only elevator company that indicated any wish whatever to handle those accounts. I think there has been a change of heart there, because we received no such offer this time.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I do not know whether or not there was a change of heart-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Order. I think perhaps it is my duty to point out to the committee, before this interesting discussion goes further along these lines, that we are dealing with a financial or money bill, and that in the bill we are bound by the terms of the resolution which preceded it. That resolution read in part as follows:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide, by way of a guarantee for bank loans . . .
Grain
I say with some regret-because this is an interesting discussion-that I do not think, under that resolution, we now have the authority to discuss alternative methods of making the funds available to farmers. Those alternatives were discussed at great length on the resolution. I feel obliged to say that we are now bound not by the words of this bill but by the general principle of the bill, and that our job is to go over the wording of it clause by clause and to decide whether those clauses shall pass or not pass or be amended.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was not endeavouring to open up a discussion that had already taken place, and I was not endeavouring to discuss the advantages or disadvantages-whatever hon. members might think-of a system of providing advances or loans or whatever you might wish to call them through the elevator companies. But when there is a provision that the government shall guarantee 10 per cent of the aggregate loans to the banks, I think it is relevant to ask questions and to point out- depending upon the type of answers that may be given-that some other alternative might have been available that would have made it possible for the government to make a much smaller guarantee.
When we are discussing the guarantee, which is 10 per cent, if it is true that an elevator company at any time in the past has offered to take a much lower guarantee, it seems to me that pointing out that fact, if it is a fact, is certainly relevant to this bill and to this section. The treasury is committed to a certain guarantee. Surely it is the duty of members of parliament to explore the situation and find out whether there was an alternative that would have provided for a much smaller guarantee.
The suggestion has been made by a number of hon. members that since this is an ironclad guarantee by the government, the banks should be prepared to reduce their interest rate from 5 per cent to 3 per cent or something in that neighbourhood. If some other facilities had been used, even if a service charge had to be added to the 3 per cent, it is my opinion that we could have made advances to farmers at an interest below 5 per cent, or else at an interest rate below 5 per cent through the facilities that they are ordinarily accustomed to use. They would be just as much opposed to paying one body an interest rate as they would be to paying any other body. But had other facilities been used, certainly there would have been much more convenience in dealing with this type of thing than there is by using the banks and the guarantee.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. In the debate on Bill No. 82 this afternoon the hon. member for Rosthern said that members of the C.C.F. had called Mr. Parker of Manitoba a rat. I was one of those who echoed the Tory interjection "He is a rat". I thought the reference was to the hon. member who had the floor, namely the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Weselak). I did not have any intention of calling the elected head of the Manitoba wheat pool and the friend of the Minister of Trade and Commerce any names whatsoever.
Since that time, Mr. Speaker, it has been pointed out to me that it is unparliamentary to call even a member of this house a rat, and I therefore withdraw that remark.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. REGIER-REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE THIS DAY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on the question of privilege, I believe I understood the hon. member to suggest that he was merely reechoing a Tory sentiment. I am sitting on the extreme left of the so-called Tory group in this house, and I would like to state quite emphatically that the interjection referred to by the hon. member came from the quarter farther left than where I sit.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. REGIER-REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE THIS DAY
speechtext: I suggest to the house that perhaps this afternoon nobody intentionally called anybody else a rat, and if they did it is to be considered withdrawn.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. REGIER-REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE THIS DAY
speechtext: As a matter of fact, I raised the point so that whoever did say it could rise in his place and say that he did not intend to cast any aspersion. When I pointed out that this was an unwarranted aspersion on a great Manitoba citizen and that it should be stricken from the record there was not a word from the C.C.F. opposition.

speechtext:
1.	What are the names of the plenipotentiaries representing Canada in connection with the Great Lakes Fisheries Convention Act?
2.	What are the names of the personnel of the Canadian section of the great lakes fisheries commission mentioned in article II of the act?
3.	What progress to date has been reported from the Canadian commission to the Department of Fisheries?
4.	What are the different methods used by the commission to combat the lamprey eel menace?
5.	Have there been any chemical control tests made towards combating the lamprey eel? If so, what results have been obtained?
6.	Since the act was passed, what work has been carried on in lake Huron and Georgian bay towards combating the lamprey eel menace?
Answer by: Mr. Sinclair:
1.	A. D. P. Heeney; Stewart Bates.
2.	Dr. A. L. Pritchard; Dr. W. J. K. Hark-ness; Dr. A. O. Blackhurst.
3.	The commission has not yet held its first meeting as the United States commissioners have only recently been appointed.
4.	The action to be taken by the commission cannot be forecast, but up to the present the following control methods are or have been in use on both the Canadian and United States sides of the lakes:
(a)	Electrical barriers in spawning streams;
(b)	Mechanical barriers in spawning streams (nets and dams);
(c)	Habitat change; gravel beds required for spawning are removed or covered with other material such as cement;
(d)	Application of materials toxic to lamprey.
5.	Yes. Results have been favourable in areas where young lamprey are congregated in streams. No material yet available for economical treatment of whole river systems. United States investigators have recently discovered specific poisons which will kill immature lampreys in the streams and not affect

other fish. Results of experiments and assessment of costs in this respect have not yet been released.
6.	The act came into force concurrent with ratification of the treaty only in October last, and there are no significant lamprey runs in the winter. One electrical barrier on Thessa-lon river and trap-nets on several small streams flowing into the north channel and Georgian bay will be operated again next summer.
